case_source: (From the order dated 08.11.2021 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.10075 of 2021)
full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan, J. This Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal (CPLA) is directed against the order dated 08.11.2021 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.10075 of 2021 staying the operation of the impugned memo No.14.00.0000.006.27. 016.19.256 dated 24.10.2021 (Annexure-I to the writ petition). 

2. The writ-petitioner-respondent No.1 filed the Writ Petition No.10075 of 2021 challenging the notification vide memo No.14.00. 0000.006.99.001.21.07 dated 06.01.2021 issued under signature of the respondent No.4 giving retirement to writ-petitioner-respondent No.1 in the post of Additional Director General (Grade-2) under section 43(1) of the সরকারী চাকুরী আইন, ২০১৮ without granting Post Retirement Leave (PRL) with other attending benefits as required under section 47 of the সরকারী চাকুরী আইন, ২০১৮ and the memo No.14.00.0000.006.27.016.19.256 dated 24.10.2021 issued by the respondent No.4 asking the writ-petitioner-respondent No.1 to show cause as to why compensation should not be realized from the pension, gratuity of the petitioner and rest under Public Demand Recovery(PDR) Act as per Rule 247 of the BSR, Part-1 and also praying for a direction upon the writ-respondents to grant writ-petitioner- respondent No.1 PRL with all attending benefits from 09.01.2021 to 08.01.2022 and then all other service benefits i.e. pension, gratuity etc. having allowed him to go on normal retirement. 

3. The facts leading to the filing of the Writ Petition are that the writ-petitioner-respondent No.1 was appointed as Assistant Post Master General cum Post Master qualifying in the BCS (Posts) Cadre in 1985 and joined in the Directorate of Posts. He was promoted to the post of Additional Director General, Grade-3 on 31.03.2013 and on 14.12.2017 he was given current charge to the post of Additional Director General (Grade-2) and on 27.02.2019 he was given promotion to the post of Additional Director General, Grade-2. On 13.03.2019 the immediate past Director General of the Directorate of Posts Mr. Susanta Kumar Mondal sent a proposal to the writ respondent No.1-petitioner No.1 for posting the writ-petitioner-respondent No.1 as Director General being the most senior and competent officer and in the said proposal the then Director General praised the writ-petitioner. Thereafter, on 03.04.2019 the writ-petitioner-respondent No.1 was given current charge to the post of Director General of the Directorate of Posts by notification vide memo No.14.00.0000.006.11.003.19.84 dated 03.04.2019 and accordingly the writ-petitioner joined the said post. The writ-petitioner- respondent No.1 performed his duty as Director General (Current Charge) with utmost sincerity and honesty without any blemish. But all of a sudden the writ-respondent No.1 the present petitioner No.1 sent the writ-petitioner on forced leave by letter dated 09.11.2020 without assigning any reason. As per S.S.C. Certificate the writ-petitioner's date of birth is on 09.01.1962 and accordingly he was supposed to go on retirement on 09.01.2021 with one year PRL at the age of superannuation as per provision of section 47 of the সরকারী চাকুরী আইন, ২০১৮. Accordingly the writ-petitioner on 21.12.2020 applied to the writ-respondent No.1 the present petitioner No.1 for granting him PRL for a period of one year from 09.01.2021. During pendency of the writ-petitioner's application for PRL, on 30.12.2020 the writ-respondent No.4 arbitrarily cancelled the earlier notification issued vide memo No.14.00.0000.006.11.003.19.84 dated 03.04.2019 by which current charge was given to the writ-petitioner to the post of Director General and thereby the current charge held by the writ petitioner No.1 in the post of Director General was cancelled without assigning any reason. The writ-respondent No.4 by notification vide memo no. 14.00.0000.006.99.001.21.07 dated 06.01.2021 granted the writ-petitioner retirement as per section 43(1)(Ka) of the সরকারী চাকুরী আইন, ২০১৮. Even after filing application for PRL, no PRL and other attending benefits were granted to the writ-petitioner-respondent No.1 till date in violation of provision of section 47 of the সরকারী চাকুরী আইন, ২০১৮. After granting direct retirement the respondents-petitioners initiated the departmental proceeding directing the writ-petitioner-respondent No.1 to appear before inquiry committee. The writ-respondents created mental pressure upon the writ-petitioner, ousted him from government residence within 30 (thirty) days and forcefully took his government vehicle within 2(two) days. The writ-respondents-petitioners issued a show cause notice on 24.10.2021 for realization of compensation in the form of punishment and as such, the writ-petitioner finding no other alternative and efficacious remedy filed the writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. Since writ-petitioner-respondent No.1 retired from service on 08.01.2021, he had no scope of exhausting jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunals. While the petitioner was Additional Director General (Planning) he was given the additional charge of Project Director of the Post e-Centre for Rural Community vide office order dated 08.12.2014. The Post e-Centre for Rural Community was one of the most priority based projects of the Government under direct supervision and control of the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology and the Office of the Prime Minister. The project was successfully completed in the year 2017. But a vested group was always against the petitioner and they had been trying to oust the petitioner from the project as they failed to get financial benefit from the project. At their instance a daily national newspaper namely the ‘Daily Inqilab’ had published several reports against the petitioner and some other officers and employees of the said project. Some other vested group complained to the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) that some irregularity and corruption were committed in the said project. On the basis of such complaint the ACC inquired into the allegation and concluded the inquiry holding that no allegation was proved in the inquiry against the writ-petitioner, accordingly the ACC disposed of the complaint by office order dated 09.07.2019 and that was duly intimated to all the concerned departments including the writ-respondent No.1 petitioner No.1. But even after getting no proof of the allegation by the ACC a vested quarter did not refrain themselves from propagatory activities against the writ-petitioner-respondent No.1. At the instance of some other dishonest officers of the Posts department the Daily Inqilab newspaper published some propagatory news involving the writ-petitioner and others. On the basis of the report of the newspaper departmental proceeding was initiated against the writ-petitioner and charge sheet was issued on 19.11.2020 i.e. before 1 month 20 days of the issuance of the impugned retirement order. On that very day the writ-petitioner was not on effective duty due to sending him on forced leave which is a clear violation of the Rule 247 of the Bangladesh Service Rules, Part-1. However, the writ-petitioner submitted his reply and an inquiry committee was formed and before the inquiry committee the petitioner appeared for hearing, but he was not allowed to cross-examine- the witnesses. The petitioner was sent on forced leave on 09.11.2020 and the departmental proceeding was initiated on 20.11.2020 when the petitioner was not on effective duty and as such the prior permission of the Hon'ble President of the Republic was required as per Rule 247 of the Bangladesh Service Rules, Part-1 for instituting the proceeding against the relinquished employee, but that mandatory provision was not followed by the respondents petitioners. 

4. The writ-petitioner was granted retirement on 06.01.2021 with effect from 08.01.2021. On 24.10.2021 the respondent No.4 issued a show cause notice upon the writ-petitioner to show cause as to why part of amount of Taka 92.87 crore (ninety two crore eighty seven lacs taka only) should not be realized from his pension and gratuity as per Rule 247 of BSR, Part-1 and rest of the financial losses should not be recovered under PDR Act for wasting government money and damaging revenue. In the said show cause notice it is stated that the allegations of corruption, negligence and misconduct were proved under Rule 32(Kha) of the সরকারী চাকুরী আইন, ২০১৮ and Rule 3(Kha) and 3(Ga)(e) of the Government Servant (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 2018, but no punishment could be awarded due to his retirement from service on 08.01.2021. The writ-petitioner applied for time to reply to the show cause notice. Though all other officers and employees of the respondents-petitioners have been enjoying the PRL as per provision of section 7 of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act, 1974 as well as সরকারী চাকুরী আইন, ২০১৮ the respondents-petitioners have denied to give the PRL and other attending leave benefits to the writ-petitioner, which is a gross discrimination on the part of the respondents-petitioners. The immediate past Director General of the Directorate of Posts Mr. Susanta Kumar Mondal has also granted PRL by notification No.14.00.0000.006.99.00319.64 dated 11.03.2019 and the writ-petitioner was posted as Director General (current charge) with effect from 03.04.2019 after his retirement. While the impugned order was passed the writ-petitioner was on forced leave and on 20.12.2020 the writ-petitioner applied for granting him PRL with effect from 09.01.2021 for a period of 1(one) year with attending benefits, but the respondent No.1-petitioner No.1 without considering the said application of the writ-petitioner and without assigning any reason sent the writ-petitioner on direct retirement as per section 43(1) of the সরকারী চাকুরী আইন, ২০১৮ in violation of provision of section 47 of the সরকারী চাকুরী আইন, ২০১৮ and as such the impugned order has been passed in violation of the mandatory provision of law and the same is also arbitrary and malafide. 

5. It is the case of the respondent that all other officers and employees of the Directorate of Posts and other offices of the government have been enjoying PRL as per provision of section 247. The immediate past Director General of the Directorate of Posts Mr. Susanta Kumar Mondal was also granted PRL, but the writ-petitioner's PRL and other allowances have been denied and thereby the writ-petitioner has been grossly discriminated by the respondents-petitioners and as such the impugned order of retirement without granting PRL with attending benefits is liable to be declared illegal and without lawful authority. 

6. Upon hearing the writ petition a Division Bench of the High Court Division on 08.11.2021 issued Rule and stayed the operation of the impugned memo No.14.00.0000.006.27.016.19.256 dated 24.10.2021. 

7. Mr. A.M. Amin Uddin, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners took us through the order of the High Court Division dated 08.11.2021, the materials on record and submits that the High Court Division erred in law by passing the impugned order of stay in as much as the writ-petitioner- respondent No.1 retired from the post of the Additional Director General (Grade-2) of the Directorate of Posts, which is the service of the Republic and the matter in issue involves terms and condition of service. According to section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 the Administrative Tribunal has the only exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights, or in respect of any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic and as such the Writ Petition No.10075 of 2021, which is now pending in the Hon'ble High Court Division is not at all maintainable and as such the impugned order of stay dated 08.11.2021 is liable to be set aside. Referring to the decision in the case of Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and others Vs. Sontosh Kumar Saha and others 21 BLC(AD) (2016) 94 the learned Advocate for the petitioner-writ respondent No.1 submits that according to Article 117 of the Constitution of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh Administrative Tribunal has the exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine the issues in respect of the terms and conditions of service of the Republic and without considering the same, the High Court Division passed the impugned order. 

8. On the other hand, Mr. Probir Neogi, the learned senior Advocate on behalf of the respondents-writ petitioners submits that the High Court Division rightly issued Rule and stayed the operation of the memo No.14.00.0000.006.27.016.19.256 dated 24.10.2021 issued by the respondent No.5. He further submits referring the case of Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Social Welfare, Bangladesh Secretariat and others Vs. Md. Akterun Nabi 71 DLR(AD)(2019) 319 that it is against the principle of natural justice to ask the writ-petitioner-respondent No.1 to pay the service related benefit for the alleged excess 2 years as the writ-petitioner-respondent No.1 was never served with any notice and was not given any opportunity of being heard. Over and above when any person renders service to anybody he has a right to get remuneration for the service he rendered and it is the duty of the party who received such service to pay for such service he received. On reply learned Attorney General further submits that if the writ petitioner has any grievance against the action of the authority he must go to the Administrative Tribunal. As we drew attention of the learned Attorney General regarding the decision reported in 71 DLR(AD)319 (paragraph-24) regarding maintainability of the writ petition on behalf of a retired public servant the learned Attorney General submits that part of the said decision has been given in contrary to the statutory provision of law as mentioned in section 4(3) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980. Possibly at the time of hearing of the case reported in 71 DLR(AD) 319 the latest provision of law was not brought to the notice of the Court. Had it been brought to notice of the Court the said decision might not been passed. 

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned advocates for the both sides, perused the order dated 08.11.2021 passed by the High Court Division, and the materials on record. 

10. It would be benefited for all of us, if we go through the powers and jurisdiction of Administrative Tribunal as has been mentioned in section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 which provides as follows: 
“4. Jurisdiction of Administrative Tribunals- 
(1) An Administrative Tribunal shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine applications made by any person in the service of the Republic (or of any statutory public authority in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights, or in respect of any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority). 
(2) A person in the service of the Republic (or of any statutory public authority) may make an application to an Administrative Tribunal under sub-section (1), if he is aggrieved by any order or decision in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights or by any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic (or of any statutory public authority). 
Provided that no application in respect of an order, decision or action which can be set aside, varied or modified by a higher administrative authority under any law for the time being in force relating to the terms and conditions of the service of the Republic (or of any statutory public authority) or the discipline of that service can be made to the Administrative Tribunal until such higher authority has taken a decision on the matter. 
Provided further that, where no decision on an appeal or application for review in respect of an order, decision or action referred to in the preceding proviso has been taken by the higher administrative authority within a period of two months from the date on which the appeal or application was preferred or made, it shall, on the expiry of such period, be deemed, for the purpose of making an application to the Administrative Tribunals under this section, that such higher authority has disallowed the appeal or the application). 
Provided further that no such application shall be entertained by the Administrative Tribunal unless it is made within six months from the date of making or taking of the order, decision or action concerned or making of the decision on the matter by the higher administrative authority, as the case may be. 
(3) In this section "person in the service of the Republic (or of any statutory public authority)" includes a person who is or has retired or is dismissed, removed or discharged from such service but does not include a person in the defence services of Bangladesh (or of the Bangladesh Rifles)." 

11. From the above provision of law it is abundantly clear that administrative tribunal has the exclusive jurisdiction to deal with the matters when a person in the service of the Republic is aggrieved by any order or decision in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights or by any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic. In the present case, the writ-petitioner-respondent No.1 is a person in the service of the Republic as per the provision of section 4(3) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 and as such the Tribunal has the exclusive jurisdiction to deal with the matter regarding the terms and conditions of the service of the writ petitioner-respondent No.1. 

12. We find substance in the submissions of the learned Attorney General regarding the case reported in 71 DLR(AD)[2019]319 in respect of maintainability of the writ petition. For the reason that the decision regarding maintainability of the writ petition filed by a retired government servant mentioned in paragraph-24 of the said judgment wherein it has been held that “we are of the view that since the order impugned before the High Court Division had been issued after retirement of the writ-petitioner-respondent he cannot be treated in the service of the Republic.” The said decision was given referring another decision in the case of Syed Abdul Ali Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Cabinet Affairs, Establishment Division and ors. reported in 31DLR (AD)[1979]256. In the said case the judgment was pronounced on February 6, 1979 and the judgment of the case reported in 71 DLR(AD)319 was pronounced on 23rd April, 2019. During this long gap of time from 1980 to 2019 the law has been changed. The sub-section 3 of section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 has been added in the said provision of law in the year 1984 vide Ordinance No.LX of 1984. When the judgment of the case reported in 31 DLR(AD)256 was pronounced at that time sub-section 3 of section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 had no existence, but when the judgment was pronounced in the case reported in 71 DLR(AD) 319 the provision of sub-section 3 of section 4 of the said Act came into force and found place in the statute book. Thus, we are of the view that the part of the judgment reported in 71 DLR(AD)319 particularly in paragraph 24 regarding maintainability of the writ petition was passed without considering the latest provision of law and, as such, the part of the said judgment regarding maintainability of the writ petition filed by a retired public servant is a per incuriam decision. 

13. What is the meaning of per incuriam? Per incuriam, literally translated as “through lack of care” is a device within the common law system of judicial precedent. A finding of per incuriam means that a previous Court judgment has failed to pay attention to relevant statutory provision or precedents. The significance of a judgment having been decided per incuriam is that it need not be followed by any equivalent Court. Ordinarily, the rationes of a judgment is binding upon all sub-ordinate Courts in similar cases. However, any Court equivalent to the Court which pronounced the judgment per incuriam is free to depart from a decision of that Court where that earlier judgment was decided per incuriam. 

14. The Court of Appeal in Morelle Ltd v. Wakeling [1955] 2 QB 379 stated that “as a general rule the only cases in which decisions should be held to have given per incuriam are those of decisions given in ignorance or forgetfulness of some inconsistent statutory provision or of some authority binding on the court concerned: so that in such cases some part of the decision or some step in the reasoning on which it is based is found, on that account, to be demonstrably wrong.” 

15. The exception of per incuriam under the doctrine of precedents can be understood in two ways. Per incuriam means “carelessness”, although in practice it is understood as per ignoratium, meaning ignorance of law. When courts ignore law and proceed to pass judgment, the said decision falls under the spectrum of per incuriam and does not necessarily need to be followed. 

16. In the case of Hyder Consulting (UK) Limited Vs. Governor, State of Orissa reported in (2015) Supreme Court Cases 189 their Lordships held that- 
“A decision can be said to be given per incuriam when the court of record has acted in ignorance of any previous decision of its own, or a subordinate court has acted in ignorance of a decision of the court of record. As regards the judgments of the Supreme Court rendered per incuriam, it cannot be said that the Supreme Court has “declared the law” on a given subject-matter, if the relevant law was not duly considered by the Supreme Court in its decision.” 

17. In the case of Dr. Shah Faesal and ors. Vs. Union of India and anr., judgment delivered on 02.03.2020 by the Supreme Court of India in Writ Petition (Civil) No.1099 of 2019, their Lordships held that- 
“A decision or judgment can also be per incuriam if it is not possible to reconcile its ratio with that of a previously pronounced judgment of a coequal or larger Bench; or if the decision of a High Court is not in consonance with the views of this Court. It must immediately be clarified that the per incuriam Rule is strictly and correctly applicable to the ratio decidendi and not to obiter dicta. 
The problem of judgment per incurim when actually arises, should present no difficulty as this Court can lay down the law afresh, if two or more of its earlier judgments cannot stand together.” 

18. Since the judgment report in 71 DLR(AD) 319 was delivered without considering the latest statutory provision (section 4(3) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980) this judgment is a judgment per incuriam. As per decision given in the case of Dr. Shah Faesal and ors. Vs. Union of India and anr. in Writ Petition (Civil) No.1099 of 2019, since it has come to the knowledge of this Court that the previous judgment reported in 71 DLR(AD) 319 was delivered due to ignorance of the statutory provision of section 4(3) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980. This Court should address the matter in accordance with law. We are of the view that it is the duty of this Court to make it very clear that if any judgment passed by the Court of co-equal jurisdiction has been passed on carelessness, or due to non-consideration of any statutory provision or previous judgment it must rectify the error. 

19. We are of the view that the ratio decided in the case of Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Social Welfare, Bangladesh Secretariat and others Vs. Md. Akterun Nabi reported in 71 DLR(AD) 319 in respect of maintainability of the writ petition by a retired public servant is not applicable in this case as the said judgment is pronounced per incuriam. 

20. In the jurisdiction of UK in many cases it has been observed that per incuriam judgment should not be followed by any equal Court even by the subordinate Court. We are unable to accept this proposition in toto. As per provision of Article 111 of the Constitution the law declared by the Appellate Division is binding upon the High Court Division and all other subordinate Courts and the law declared by the High Court Division is binding upon all the subordinate Courts. In the case of Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) vs. Abdul Barek Dewan being dead his heirs: Bali Begum and others reported in 4 BLC(AD)85 their Lordships held that “The word “per incuriam” is a Latin expression. It means through inadvertence. A decision can be said generally to be given per incuriam when the court had acted in ignorance of a previous decision of its own or when the High Court Division had acted in ignorance of a decision of the Appellate Division. [see Punjab Land Development and Reclamation Corporation Ltd. vs Presiding Officer, Labour Court, 1990(3)SCC685(705)]. Nothing could be shown that the Appellate Division in deciding the said case had overlooked any of its earlier decision on the point. So, it was not open to the High Court Division to describe it as one given “per incuriam”. Even if it were so, it could not have been ignored by the High Court Division in view of Article 111 of the Constitution which embodies, as a rule of law, the doctrine of precedent. 

21. Apart from the provision of Article 111 of the Constitution enjoining upon all courts below to obey the law laid down by this Court, judicial discipline requires that the High Court Division should follow the decision of the Appellate Division and that it is necessary for the lower tiers of courts to accept the decision of the higher tiers as a binding precedent. This view was poignantly highlighted in Cassell & Co. Ltd vs Broome and another, (1972) AC 1027 where Lord Hailsham of St. Marylebone, the Lord Chancellor, in his judgment said: 
“The fact is, and I hope it will never be necessary to say so again, that, in the hierarchical system of courts which exists in this country, it is necessary for each lower tier, including the Court of Appeal, to accept loyally the decisions of the higher tiers.” 

22. The provision of Article 111 of the Constitution runs a follows: 
“The law declared by the Appellate Division shall be binding on the High Court Division and the law declared by either division of the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts subordinate to it.” 

23. In view of the above judgment reported in 4 BLC(AD) 85, if any judgment pronounced by the Appellate Division, as per provision of Article 111 of the Constitution the High Court Division is not competent to say the judgment is per incuriam. Primarily the High Court Division must follow the judgment in toto, however, in such a situation the High Court Division may draw attention of the Hon’ble Chief Justice regarding the matter. On the other hand even if any judgment is pronounced by the High Court Division, the subordinate Courts have no jurisdiction to raise any question regarding the legality of the judgment on the point of per imcuriam. Parties may get remedy on preferring appeal. 

24. In view of the above discussions and considering other materials on record, we are of the view that the High Court Division committed illegality in issuing Rule and passing an order staying the operation of the impugned memo No.14.00.0000.006.27. 016.27.016.19.256 dated 24.10.2021. 

25. In the light of the observations made above, we find merit in the submissions of the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioners and therefore the Rule issued by the High Court Division is liable to be discharged. 

26. Hence, the Rule issued by the High Court Division on 08.11.2021 is discharged. However, the petitioners are directed to issue a fresh notice upon the respondent No.1 giving him opportunity to submit his reply and then to dispose of the matter in accordance with law. 

Accordingly, the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal is disposed of. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mahmudul Hoque, J.: On an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure this Rule Was issued at the instance of the petitioner calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-2 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 31-7-2007 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Sylhet in title Appeal No. 01 of 2003 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 18-8-2002 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 220 of 1999 decreeing the suit in part should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2, as plaintiff, instituted Title Suit No. 220 of 1999 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet for declaration of title in respect of the land described in Schedule No. 1 and further declaration that two registered deeds described in Schedule No. 3 are illegal, ineffective, concocted and not binding upon the plaintiffs, stating that the suit land measuring an area of 1-47 acres appertaining to Plot Nos. 1051 and 1052 under SA Khatian Nos. 171 and 225 respectively, originally belonged to one Rash Moni Das alias Rash Ram Das and Bishnu Charan Das and their names stood recorded in khatian in equal share. Rash Ram Das died leaving behind two sons namely, Umesh Chandra Das and Promesh Chandra Das and they became owners of half of the land i.e. 0.73½ acre. While they were in possession of the same, sold out 0.47 acre land to one Farmuz Ali, predecessor of the plaintiffs and proforma-defendant No. 4, by a registered deed of sale dated 5-6-1970, Said Farmuz Ali while in possession of the same sold out the whole 47 decimals of land to one Abdur Rob by a registered deed of sale dated 21-4-1980 and said Abdur Rob while in enjoyment sold out the same to the plaintiffs and the proforma defendant No. 4 by a registered deed of sale dated 5-7-1987. Said Bishnu Charan Das while in possession sold out his entire share i.e. 73½ decimals of land to the plaintiffs and the proforma defendant No. 4 by a registered deed of sale dated 13-12-1988. Said Umesh Chandra Das and Promesh Chandra Das thereafter sold their remaining 26½ decimals of land to one Yogya Ram Das who got possession and enjoyed the same. Thereafter, Yogya Ram Das sold out 3½ decimals of land therefrom to the plaintiffs and defendant No. 4 by a registered deed of sale dated 15-2-1989 and sold out the rest 23 decimals to Mohesh Chandra Das and Mohim Chandra Das who sold out the same to Nobo Kumar Das by a registered deed of sale dated 1-4-1998. Against the said transfer the plaintiffs filed Pre-emption Case No. 15 of 1998 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Kanaighat, Sylhet which was allowed in favour of the preemptors i.e. the plaintiffs. In the aforesaid way the plaintiffs and proforma-defendant No. 4 has acquired title in the whole 1.47 acres of land of the suit plots and they have been possessing the same. The defendant No. 1 has no right, title or interest in the suit land. Nevertheless, the defendant No. 1 has created 2(two) registered deeds by which Mohesh Chandra and Mohim Chandra transferred 39 decimals of land in favour of the defendant No. 1. Those two deeds have also clouded the title of the plaintiffs, as such, the plaintiffs have become compelled to file the instant suit.

3. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit through his constituted attorney by filing a written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending inter alia, that one Mohim Chandra Das and Mohesh Chandra Das were the owners of the suit land including other lands and while they were enjoying and possessing the said land, declared to sell the same and the defendant No. 1 agreed to purchase and accordingly, a bainanama was executed in respect of the suit land and delivered possession of the same. The defendant No. 1 has been enjoying and possessing the suit land with the knowledge of all and after payment of the rest consideration money Mohim Chandra Das and Mohesh Chandra Das executed and registered two separate deeds of sale. The plaintiffs were aware about the execution of the bainapatra but only to harass this defendant, the instant suit has been filed. The plaintiffs are very clever men and making some false statement they have filed the instant suit, moreover, in respect of the suit land the plaintiffs have filed Pre-emption Case No. 19 of 1998 which is still pending for disposal. The defendant No. 1 resides in abroad and while the plaintiffs were trying to take possession of the suit land forcefully a Non FIR Case No. 19 of 1998 was filed against them and in the said case police submitted report to the effect that the defendant is in possession of the case land. Making some false statements and concealing the real facts the plaintiffs have filed the instant suit and they have/had no right, title, interest or possession over the suit land, hence, the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs.

4. The trial court by the judgment and decree dated 18-8-2002 decreed the suit in part and declared title of the plaintiffs and proforma-defendant No. 4 in respect of 1.28¼ acres of land described in Schedule No. 1 and also declared the two deeds in question are not binding upon the plaintiffs. Against the judgment and decree dated 18-8-2002, the plaintiffs filed Title Appeal No. 01 of 2003 before the learned District Judge, Sylhet and the same was heard by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Sylhet, on transfer, who by the impugned judgment and decree dated 31-7-2007 allowed the appeal and decreed the suit in full as prayed for. At this stage, the petitioner moved this Court by filing this revisional application and obtained the present Rule and order of stay.

5. Mr. M. Mushfiqur Rahman, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that admittedly, the property in question originally belonged to Rash Ram Das and Bishnu Charan Das in equal share measuring 73½ sataks each. Bishnu Charan transferred his half share to the plaintiffs and proforma-defendant No. 4 by a registered deed dated 13-12-1988. Rash Ram Das died leaving 2(two) sons, Umesh Chandra Das and Promesh Chandra Das who got 73½ sataks out of which they transferred 47 sataks of land to Farmuz Ali, father of the plaintiffs by a registered deed dated 5-6-1970. The rest 26½ sataks land was transferred to one Yogya Ram Das. He transferred 3¼ sataks to the plaintiffs and proforma-defendant No. 4 by a registered deed dated 15-2-1989 and rest 23 sataks of land to Mohesh Chandra Das and Mohim Chandra Das by a registered deed dated 1-4-1998. Said 23 sataks was preempted by the plaintiffs in Preemption Case No. 15 of 1998 on 29-8-1999 but before the deed under preemption the petitioner purchased 39 sataks of land by 2(two) separate deeds dated 26-3-1998 from Mohesh Chandra and Mohim Chandra against which the plaintiffs filed Preemption Case No. 19 of 1998 which was ultimately failed, therefore, the petitioner by the said deeds dated 26-3-1998 Exhibits 6 and 6(ka) at least acquired 23 sataks of land in the suit plots, but the trial court wrongly held that the defendant No. 1 acquired 18 sataks only and the appellate court on a misconception of law wrongly decreed the suit for entire land, taking into consideration that the deed of Nabo Kumar though executed later but registered on 1-4-1998 i.e. earlier of the deeds registered on 5-4-1998. So, it will get preference over the deed registered on 5-4-1998, as such, both the courts below committed error of law, misread and misconstrued the documents occasioning failure of justice.

6. Mr. Uzzal Bhowmik for Mr. Didar Alam Kollol, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 at the very outset submits that Promesh Chandra Das and Umesh Chandra Das transferred 47 sataks of land to Farmuz Ali, father of the plaintiffs on 5-6-1970, he subsequently, transferred the Same to one Abdur Rob by a registered deed dated 22-4-1980, thereafter, the plaintiffs and proforma-defendant No. 4 by a registered deed dated 5-7-1987 purchased the said 47 sataks of land from Abdur Rob, therefore, Farmuz Ali had no transferable title in the suit property to transfer the same to Mohesh Chandra Das and Mohim Chandra Das on 4-6-1989, as such, by the deeds dated 26-3-1998 the petitioner-defendant acquired no title in the suit property, the trial court upon misconception of law and misconstruction of the evidences both oral and documentary decreed the suit in part for 1.28½ acres and giving 18 sataks of land to the petitioner. He further submits that the petitioner did not aggrieve against the judgment and decree of the trial court and no appeal preferred by them. It is also argued that on appeal preferred by the plaintiffs, the appellate court rightly decreed the suit in full finding no title of the defendant in the suit property, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

7. Heard the learned Advocates of both the parties, have gone through the revisional application, plaint, written statement, evidences both oral and documentary available in the lower court records and the impugned judgment and decree of both the courts below.

8. As admitted by the parties, suit plot Nos. 1051 and 1052 measuring 1-47 sataks belonged to Rash Ram Das and Bishnu Charan Das in equal share measuring 73 1/2 sataks each. Rash Ram Das died leaving 2(two) sons, Umesh Chandra Das and Promesh Chandra Das who transferred 47 sataks of land to one Farmuz Ali, father of plaintiffs, by a sale deed dated 5-6-1970 (Exhibit 3). Farmuz Ali subsequently, transferred the same to one Abdur Rob by a registered deed dated 22-4-1980 (Exhibit 4). The plaintiffs claim that they purchased the said property from Abdur Rob by a sale deed dated 5-7-1987 (Exhibit 1(Ka). Said Deed No. 5161 dated 5-07-1987 in original has been filed by the plaintiffs which shows that they purchased 15 sataks of land from Plot No. 1051 under Khatian No. 172 and 32 sataks from Plot No. 1228 under Khatian No. 238 and by the said deed no property was purchased by them from Plot No. 1052. However, said Plot No. 1052 contains in the deed of Abdur Rob dated 22-4-1980 (Exhibit 4). After transfer to Farmuz Ali, Umesh and Promesh had 26 1/2 sataks of land which was transferred to one Yogya Ram Das as admitted by the parties but neither the plaintiffs nor the defendant filed any deed in the name of Yogya Ram Das. Said Yogya Ram Das by a sale deed dated 15-2-1989 Exhibit 6(kha) transferred 3¼ sataks of land to the plaintiffs and proforma-defendant No. 4 the rest 23 sataks of land also transferred by him to Mohesh Chandra and Mohim Chandra but no such deed has been submitted by the parties to the proceedings. Mohesh and Mohim by a sale Deed No. 2151 of 1998 dated 1-4-1998 (Exhibit Ga) transferred the same to one Nabo Kumar Das. Before the said transfer Mohesh and Mohim Chandra by 2(two) Registered Deed Nos. 2223 of 1998 and 2218 of 1998 both executed on 26-3-1998 and registered on 5-4-1998 transferred 39 sataks of land to the defendant No. 1 (Exhibits-6 and 6(Ka).

9. It appears that the plaintiffs filed Preemption Case No. 15 of 1998 in respect of sale deed dated 1-4-1998 (Exhibit 6(Ga) against Nabo Kumar, Mohesh Chandra and Mohim Chandra which was allowed on 29-8-1999 (Exhibit 5). The plaintiffs also filed another Preemption Case No. 19 of 1998 against defendant No. 1, Abdur Rouf, Mohesh Chandra and Mohim Chandra which was disallowed by the trial court on 31-7-2001. On appeal the preemption was allowed and on revision it was disallowed. Resultantly, die plaintiffs failed to succeed the preemption in respect of deeds dated 26-3-1998 in the name of defendant No. 1.

10. From the documents available in file, it appears that the plaintiffs purchased 73½ sataks of land from Bishnu Charan Das by sale deed dated 13-12-1988 (Exhibit 2), 15 sataks of land in Plot No. 1051 under Khatian No. 172 from Abdur Rob by deed dated 5-7-1987 (Exhibit l(Ka) and 3¼ sataks of land from Plot Nos. 1051 and 1052 and also claim that they got 23 sataks of land by preemption in Preemption Case No. 15 of 1998.

11. On the other hand, Mohesh Chandra and Mohim Chandra admittedly purchased the said 23 sataks of land from Yogya Ram and they by 2(two) separate sale deeds dated 26-3-1998 transferred 39 sataks of land to defendant No. 1 Abdur Rouf against which admitting those transfers present plaintiffs filed Preemption Case No. 19 of 1998 which was ultimately failed. Deed No. 2218 of 1998 (Exhibit 6) and Deed No. 2223 of 1998 (Exhibit 6(Ka) were executed on 26-3-1998 by Mohim and Mohesh in favour of the petitioner Abdur Rouf and registered on 5-4-1998 against which Preemption Case No. 19 of 1998 was failed. Said Mohim and Mohesh by another deed executed and registered on 1-4-1998 transferred 23 sataks of land in favour of one Nabo Kumar, against which the plaintiff filed Preemption Case No. 15 of 1998 which was allowed on 29-8-1999 (Exhibit 5). Exhibits-6 and 6(Ka) were executed on 26-3-1998 and registered on 5-4-1998, Exhibit 6(Ga) executed and registered on 1-4-1998. Both the courts below considered the deed dated 1-4-1998 as the same was registered earlier to the deeds dated 26-3-1998 under section 47 of the Registration Act and concurrently held that since the deed of Nabo Kumar registered earlier it will take effect from the date of registration and not from the date of execution. To appreciate the provisions of law section 47 of the Registration Act may be looked into which runs thus:
47, "Time from which registered document operates--A registered document shall operate from the time from which it would have commenced to operate if no registration thereof had been required or made, and not from the time of its registration."

12. From the language used in section 47 of the Registration Act the sale deed shall operate from the date of execution not from the date of registration. Hence, this Court finds that both the courts below wrongly held that the sale shall operate from the date of registration not from the date of execution. Therefore, the sale deeds dated 26-3-1998 shall get preference over the sale deed dated 1-4-1998 executed and registered in favour Nabo Kumar. In Preemption Case No. 15 of 1998 this petitioner-defendant was not made party, as such, the defendant No. 1 is not at all bound by the judgment and order passed in Preemption Case No. 15 of 1998.

13. It is true that the right and title whatever Farmuz Ali has had in the suit plots was transferred to Abdur Rob by a sale deed dated 22-4-1980 (Exhibit 2), as such, Farmuz Ali had no transferable interest in the property on 4-6-1989 to transfer in favour of Mohim Chandra and Mohesh Chandra. Therefore, Mohim and Mohesh acquired no title by Sale Deed No. 3931 dated 4-6-1989 (Exhibit Cha) but Mohim and Mohesh acquired title in 23 sataks of land by purchase from Yogya Ram Das which was transferred by them firstly to the defendant No. 1 by 2(two) separate sale deeds dated 26-3-1998 and secondly by a sale deed dated 1-4-1998 to Nabo Kumar. As per section 47 of the Registration Act since the sale operate from the date of execution, deed of the defendant No. 1 shall prevail over the deed of Nabo Kumar. Therefore, the defendant No. 1 by the aforesaid 2(two) deeds would be entitled to get 23 sataks of land from Plot Nos. 1051 and 1052 but both the courts below failed to appreciate the provisions of law and consider the said deeds of the defendant No. 1 in its true perspective.

14. As stated above, the plaintiffs and proforma-defendant No. 4 acquired (73½ + 15 + 3) = 91.75 sataks of land by deed dated 13-12-1988, 5-7-1987 and 15-2-1989 Exhibits-2, 1(Ka) and 6(Kha) respectively, from Plot Nos. 1051 and 1052, In Preemption Case No. 15 of 1998 though preemption was allowed in favour of plaintiffs but the deed of Nabo Kumar dated 1-4-1998 being executed later than the deed dated 26-3-1998 of the defendant No. 1, by the said deed neither Nabo Kumar nor the plaintiffs acquired any title. Therefore, said 23 sataks of land shall cover by the deeds executed by Mohim and Mohesh on 26-3-1998 in favour of defendant No. 1. In the schedule to the original Deed No. 5161 executed by Abdur Rob in favour of me plaintiffs and proforma-defendant No. 4, Plot No. 1052 is totally absent but certified copy of the same contains Plot No. 1052, Khatian No. 225 measuring 32 sataks (Exhibits 1 and 1(Ka). Learned Lawyer for the opposite-parties could not satisfy the court why there is such anomalies in the 2(two) deeds. However, by the documentary evidences available in file vendor of the defendant No. 1 by purchase from Yogya Ram Das acquired 23 sataks of land in the suit plots but they transferred 39 sataks of land from 2(two) plots in favour of defendant No. 1 by 2(two) separate deeds dated 26-3-1998 and in favour of Nabo Kumar by deed dated 1-4-1998 measuring 23 sataks totalling 62 sataks, where they have only title in 23 sataks and the same was transferred firstly, to the defendant No. 1 and secondly, to Nabo Kumar. Since the deed in favour of defendant No. 1-petitioner was executed earlier by Mohim and Mohesh and admitting the said deed the plaintiff-opposite-parties filed Preemption Case No. 19 of 1998 seeking preemption of the same but ultimately foiled, the defendant No. 1 acquired title in Plot Nos. 1051 and 1052 for 23 sataks only.

15. In view of the above, both the courts below committed error of law, consequently, the trial court decreed the suit in part for 1.28¼ sataks in favour of the plaintiffs and the appellate court decreed the suit for 1.47 sataks. From the discussions made hereinabove, this Court finds that the defendant No. 1 by purchase from Mohim and Mohesh acquired 23 sataks of land in the suit property and the plaintiffs only acquired 1.24 sataks land though there are some anomalies between the deed dated 5-7-1987 Exhibit 1(Ka) in its schedule and certified copy of the same (Exhibit 1).

16. In view of the above, this Court finds merit in the Rule and in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to costs.

18. The judgment and decree of both the courts below hereby set-aside and modified. Title Suit No. 220 of 1999 is hereby decreed in favour of the plaintiffs in part. It is hereby, declared that the plaintiffs and proforma-defendant No. 4 acquired title in 1.24 acres of land described in schedule to the plaint.

19. Order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated.

Communicate a copy of the judgment to the Court concerned and send down the lower court records at once.

End.

Vs.

full_judgment:
Md. Zakir Hossain, J.
1. Since the questions of law involved in Civil Revision No. 1109 of 2011, Civil Revision No. 1110 of 2011 and Civil Revision No. 1111 of 2011 are almost, same and identical, and parties are same; therefore, they are taken up together for hearing and be disposed of by this single judgment and the same shall govern in all the aforesaid revisional applications.

2. At the instance of the petitioner, the Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-9 of all the Revisional Applications to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 16-1-2011 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 60 of 2005, Miscellaneous Appeal No. 61 of 2005 and Miscellaneous Appeal No. 62 of 2005 reversing the judgment and order dated 19-1-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 76 of 1996, Miscellaneous Case No. 77 of 1996 and Miscellaneous Case No. 78 of 1996 respectively by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka.

3. Facts leading to the issuance of the Rule are inter alia that the petitioner as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No. 76 of 1996, Miscellaneous Case No. 77 of 1996 and Miscellaneous Case No. 78 of 1996 against the pre-emptee-opposite party Nos. 1-9 before the Court of Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act (NAT Act). Having received the summons of all the aforesaid three miscellaneous cases, the pre-emptee-opposite parties entered appearance in all the aforesaid three miscellaneous (pre-emption) cases and filed written objections denying the allegations set out therein. Thereafter, all the aforesaid miscellaneous cases were fixed for simultaneously hearing. Eventually, the pre-emptor obtained ex-parte decree in those miscellaneous (pre-emption) cases on 1-10-1995. Thereafter, the pre-emptee-opposite parties filed Miscellaneous Case No. 76 of 1996, Miscellaneous Case No. 77 of 1996 and Miscellaneous Case No. 78 of 1996 under Order IX, rule 13 of Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, in short 'the CPC' for setting aside the ex-parte judgment and orders. On 19-1-2005, those were fixed for ex-parte hearing. On that date, all the aforesaid miscellaneous cases were dismissed for default.

4. Challenging the legality and propriety of the said orders, the pre-emptee-opposite party Nos. 1-9 filed the aforesaid miscellaneous appeals before the learned District Judge, Dhaka. On transfer, me learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka heard those appeals and was pleased to allow the appeal. Questioning the legality of the judgment and orders of the aforesaid appeals, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the Rules.

5. Mr. Probir Neogi, the learned Senior Advocate along with Mr. Syed Ejaz Kabir appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that no appeal lies against an order dismissing an application made under Order IX, rule 13 of the CPC for restoration of the proceedings under section 24 of the NAT Act. Mr. Probir Neogi banks on the decision of the case of Belayet Hossain vs. Md. Abu Taher, reported in 32 DLR (AD) 231.

6. He further submits that the dismissal orders of the miscellaneous cases do not fall within the definition of decree or within the ambit of Order 43 rule 1(d) of the CPC; therefore, the aforesaid miscellaneous appeals are incompetent; hence, the Rules deserve to be made absolute.

7. Per contra, Mr. Tapan Chakraborty, the learned Advocate along with Mr. Muhammad Rafiul Islam appearing on behalf of the opposite parties Nos. 1, 3, 5, 8 and 10, submits that the High Court Division is competent to examine the judgments and orders dated 16-1-2011 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in the said miscellaneous appeals. He further submits that the ends of justice should not be defeated by mere technicalities and none can hope to score victory on such technicalities. He further submits that the learned Appellate Judge after considering the facts and circumstances of the cases rightly allowed the aforesaid miscellaneous appeals assigning cogent reasons. Therefore, they do not call for any interference. In support of his submissions, he relies on the decisions of the cases reported in 7 BLT (AD) 125, 9 MLR (AD) 285 : 9 BLC (AD) 169, 1997 BLD (AD) 205, 27 DLR (AD) 115, 26 BLC (AD) 302 and 53 DLR 29, 5 MLR (HCD) 57, 69 DLR 510, 19 BLC 743.

8. I have perused the entire materials on record thoroughly and perused the submissions of the learned Advocates and intricate question of law critically involved in this cases.

9. Now, the moot issue is--
Whether the aforesaid miscellaneous appeals are competent against the order of dismissal of the said miscellaneous cases for default.

10. Let me examine the common order passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in the three miscellaneous cases may be read thus:
"Petitioner files a petition praying to adjournment of ex-parte hearing. HD. The learned Advocate. Perused the application for adjournment and also the case record, it appears that the petitioner took 4 consecutive adjournment for ex-parte hearing. As per law the plaintiff is not entitle to get more than 3 adjournment. So the present application for adjournment be disallowed. The plaintiff is directed to get ready immediately. Thereafter, the petitioner did not take any steps. So the present miscellaneous case is liable to be dismissed. Hence. Ordered that the present miscellaneous case be dismissed for non-appearance of the plaintiff."

11. On perusal of the judgment of Belayet Hossain, supra in details it is as clear as day light that the Appellate Division came to the positive finding that dismissal of miscellaneous cases for default can be challenged by way of revision but not appeal as the dismissal order is neither a decree nor appealable order in view of Order 43 rule 1(d) of the CPC. The Appellate Division held:
"On consideration of ratio decidendi of the cited decision, we do not find any reason to take a different view and disturb the long settled decisions followed by the High Court Division and its predecessor High Court on the question for the last thirty years. Apart from the question of disturbing the stare decisis the decisions are based on good reasons. The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act does not provide for any appeal from such an order. The Civil Procedure Code provides appeal from an order rejecting application to set-aside a decree passed ex-parte made in a suit. The application of this rule pre-supposes existence to two conditions which are absent in an order so passed in a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The first is that the order of refusal is to set-aside an ex-parte decree and the second, that the order is passed in a proceeding which is a suit. None of the conditions being present, the view so long held does not call for any revision."

12. In the case of Abdur Rahman vs. Shamsun Nahar and others, reported in 7 BLT (AD) 125, it was held:
The High Court Division rightly found the pre-emptee-respondents appeal was misconceived and inadvertent and that in the revisional jurisdiction the Court was competent to examine the order dated 27-2-1990.

13. In the backdrop, I am of the view that the ratio of the aforesaid cases undoubtedly be applicable in respect of miscellaneous cases so far it relates to dismissal for default of the miscellaneous cases filed under Order 9 rule 13 of the CPC in respect of the pre-emption proceeding under section 24 of the NAT Act.

14. Now my final conclusion is that instead of filing revision, the pre-emptee preferred the said miscellaneous appeals impugning the aforesaid dismissal orders.

15. In the case of Om Prakash and others vs. Dwarka Prasad and another, reported in MANU/MP/0442/2004 : AIR 2005 MP 40, it was observed:
In the case of Bahori vs. Vidya Ram (AIR 1978 Allahabad 299), it is held that if revision is filed within limitation prescribed for appeal, then prayer for converting revision into appeal after expiry of period of limitation is maintainable. It is held that there is no specific provision for conversion of an appeal into a revision or vice versa. Consequently, the exercise of power has to be only under the provisions of section 151 of the Code. The inherent powers of the Court permit the Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice. The power is undoubtedly discretionary and is to be exercised in a proper case. If the interest of justice requires the passing of such an order or to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court, the Court would be fully justified in passing an order under this provision. It is further held that there is nothing like a period of limitation for making an application for conversion of an appeals into revision or vice versa. All that is required to be seen is if the appeal or the revision had been filed within the time prescribed for the filing of the appeal, or the revision, as the case may be. Even otherwise, there would be very few cases, were the conversion would be sought before the expiry of the period of filing the appeal. In most cases, the point would emanate after an objection had been filed or made by the other side. It would undoubtedly be open to the Court considering the question of conversion to satisfy itself that the prayer was bona fide and that there was no unusual delay.

16. Revision means reconsideration, reappraisal, re-appreciation, revaluation of the order of the Court below, so far it relates to question of law. The provision relating to filing of a revision is contained in section 115 of the Code. This section was earlier amended twice, once in 1978 and next in 1983. But major changes have been made by the amendment made in 2005 when the original section was substituted. Now, under sub-section (1), an aggrieved party may file a revision against a decree or order that has been passed by the court of District Judge, Additional district Judge or against a decree passed by a court of Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge from which no appeal lies. From the long line of decisions of the Apex Court, now almost the uniform view is that a revisional Court may exercise its power:--
(i) when there is an error of law resulting in an error which occasioned failure of justice;
(ii) when the procedure followed by the lower court was not legal;
(iii) when the lower court acted without jurisdiction, or exercised a jurisdiction not conferred by law;
(iv) when the lower court acted illegally or with material illegality in exercise of law or has committed error in procedure during the course of trial and such breach or error has affected the ultimate exercise of jurisdiction;
(v) when there is misreading of evidence, wrong appreciation of evidence, non-consideration of any legal evidence, wrong consideration of documentary evidence by the lower court, when the findings of the lower courts are found to be perverse and not based on the evidence on record which resulted in arriving at a wrong decision occasioning failure of justice.

17. There is no period of limitation for filing a revisional application. However, the established principle is that such an application is to be filed within thirty days to the Court of the learned District Judge or within ninety days to the High Court Division. It is also settled that in a suitable case, the revisional Court may also condone delay, if any. However, when the High Court Division acts suo moto, there will be no limitation.

18. It cannot be denied that the scope of appeal is wider that of revision. Appeal is a continuation of suit. Appeal may be filed challenging the question of law and facts. On the other hand, revision lies only in law point. Revisional Court will see as to whether the Court below committed an error of law causing failure of justice. All decrees are appealable save three decrees such as:-Decree passed on compromise, Decree passed under section 9 of SR Act and under the Small Causes Court Act, 1887. The decrees which are not appealable may be revisable.

19. All orders are revisable except orders listed out as appealable order under order 43 rule 1 and section 104 of CPC. In fact, where there is no appeal, there is revision.

20. In this case in hand, neither the Advocate nor the Judge of the Court below took notice as to the effect that appeal was not competent. Their bona fide mistake shall not prevent the pre-emptee-opposite parties to seek an appropriate remedy. Moreover, the wrong shopping of forum by the attorney of the parties shall not close the door of the remedy forever; therefore, I hold the view to meet the ends of justice that the appeals are required to convert into revisions and, therefore, it would be appropriate to remit the cases to the Court of the learned District Judge for disposal by converting the aforesaid miscellaneous appeals into revisions.

21. For the reasons stated above, all the Rules of Civil Revision No. 1109 of 2011, Civil Revision No. 1110 of 2011 and Civil Revision No. 1111 of 2011 are made absolute; however, without passing any order as to costs. The earlier orders of stay by this Court thus stand vacated and recalled.

22. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and orders of the aforesaid Miscellaneous Appeal No. 60 of 2005, Miscellaneous Appeal No. 61 of 2005 and Miscellaneous Appeal No. 62 of 2005 are hereby set-aside and thus, the aforesaid miscellaneous appeals are remitted back to the Court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka. Having received the copy of the judgment, the learned District Judge, Dhaka shall convert those miscellaneous appeals into revisions and further directed to dispose of the same within 120 days from the date of receiving the copy of the judgment positively.

Let a copy of the judgment be transmitted to the Court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka at once.

End.
