full_judgment:
SM Maniruzzaman, J: In this Rule Nisi, issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the respondents have been called upon to show cause as to why failure of the respondents to make final assessment of the petitioner's imported goods covered under Letter of Credit No. 086218010591 dated 30-7-2018 under Bill of Entry No. C-28719 dated 18-10-2018 within the stipulated period of 120(one hundred twenty) working days from the date of provisional assessment under the provision of section 81(2) of the Customs Act, 1969 should not be declared to have been done without lawful authority and hence, of no legal effect and also as to why a direction should not be given upon the respondents to release/return the bank guarantee being No. 48/2018 dated 22-10-2018 for Taka 15,86,504.67 (Taka fifteen lac eighty six thousand five hundred four and paisa sixty seven) lying with the respondent No. 4 and /or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. However, at the time of issuance of the Rule, the contending parties were directed to maintain status-quo in respect of encashment of the bank guarantee for a prescribed period. 

3. Facts, relevant for disposal of the Rule, in short, are that the petitioner is the proprietor of "M/s Nippon Boiler House" and is engaged in the business of importation various commodity from abroad in order to sell the same in the local market. 

4. The petitioner in course of his business, opened a Letter of Credit No. 086218010591 dated 30-7-2018 for importing "Black Steel Seamless Pipe" from South Korea under HS Code Nos. 7304.29.10 and 7304.29.20. After arrival of the goods at ICD, Kamalapur, Dhaka the petitioner however, collected shipping documents from his bank and accordingly submitted Bill of Entry being No. C-28719 dated 18-10-2018 through his C&F Agent along with those documents to the concerned customs authority for assessment and releasing the goods on payment of customs duty and taxes. Thereafter, the concerned respondent customs authority physically examined the goods and did not accept the HS Code of the goods as declared by the petitioner. Rather, determined the goods to fall under HS Code Nos. 7306.29.20 and 7306.29.10. The respondent customs authority also suggested that the goods required to be (sample) examined in the BCSIR for determining the correct applicable HS Code. In this regard, the authority concerned proposed to allow the petitioner to release the goods on provisional assessment on furnishing bank guarantee for the differential amount of duty and taxes between the declared HS Code Nos. 7304.29.10 and 7304.29.20 and the proposed HS Code Nos. 7306.29.10 and 7306.29.20 respectively. 

5. The petitioner duly accepted the said proposal of the customs authority and made payment of all customs duties and taxes as his declared HS Code in cash and furnished bank guarantee being No. 48/2018 dated 22-10-2018 for Taka 15,86,504.67 (Taka fifteen lac eighty six thousand five hundred four and paisa sixty seven) for the differential amount of duty and taxes. Pursuant thereto the customs authority released the goods on provisional assessment dated 24-10-2018. 

6. However, the categorical assertion of the petitioner is that after releasing of the goods on provisional assessment, the concerned respondent customs authority did not complete final assessment as required under section 81(2) of the Customs Act, 1969 (in short, the Act). In view of the such context, the petitioner has filed the instant writ petition challenging the inaction of the respondents failure to make final assessment of his imported goods within due time as required under the law and also seeking direction to return the bank guarantee furnished by him before the respondent customs authority as security on provisionally assessment and accordingly, obtained the present Rule along with order of statuesque. 

7. Conversely, the respondent No. 1, Commissioner of Customs, ICD, Kamalapur, Dhaka entered appearance by filing affidavit-in-opposition controverting the materials facts so made in the writ petition contending inter alia that; the petitioner imported "Black Steel Seamless Pipe" from South Korea declaring HS Code Nos. 7304.29.10 and 7304.29.20 and after physical examination of the goods found that the declared HS Codes were not correct. So, the respondent customs authority decided to assess the said "Black Steel Seamless Pipes size 3/4" x 6" and 81"" under HS Code Nos. 7306.29.20 and 7306.29.10 respectively. Thereafter, the petitioner's C&F agent on 18-10-2018 made an application to the Additional Commissioner of Customs requesting him to draw sample of the imported goods and send the same to external Lab of BCSIR for chemical examination in order to determine the actual HS Code and also requested to release the goods on accepting bank guarantee for the differential amount of duty and taxes on the basis of declared HS Code and proposed HS Code. 

8. Thereafter, the customs authority allowed the petitioner to get delivery of the goods on provisional assessment upon submitting bank guarantee for the differential amount of duty and taxes. Accordingly, the concerned respondent to assess the goods provisionally on 24-10-2018 under section 81 of the Act, 1969. Thereafter on 27-11-2018 the sample of the goods was sent to the BCSIR Lab vide Nathi No. 5th Cus(1386) Non-PSI/ Import/Group-06/18/16260(2) for chemical examination and the customs authority categorically stated therein that the cost of test would be provided by the petitioner under section 2(X) of the Act, 1969 [Annexure 2(3) of the affidavit-in-opposition]. But, the petitioner did not pay the cost of the chemical test report to the BCSIR. The respondent customs authority after being informed not paying the said test fee by the petitioner, then the respondent No. 2 further informed the petitioner vide letter dated 10-4-2019 [Annexure 2(4) of the affidavit-in-opposition] requesting to take necessary steps to deposit chemical test fee to the authority of BCSIR within 10 days. But, the petitioner without making payment of chemical test fee as per his undertaking, most illegally and inalafide intention filed the instant writ petition and obtained the present Rule and order of statuesque. 

9. Countering the said contention of the respondent, the petitioner filed affidavit-in-reply contending further that section 200 of the Act, 1969 is mere declaratory in a nature not mandatory. The concerned respondent sent a letter to the petitioner asking to pay the cost of the chemical test within 120(one hundred twenty) working days from the date of provisional assessment is also misconceived and incorrect, because the letter was sent on 10-4-2019 after expiry of 120(one hundred twenty) working days. 

10. Mr Md Saiful Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the respondent customs authority miserably failed to make final assessment of the imported goods of the petitioner as per the specific provision of law, in as much as, section 81 of the Act, 1969 clearly stipulates to make final assessment of goods within 120 (one hundred and twenty) working days from the date of provisional assessment and the concerned respondents having failed to make final assessment of the imported goods of the petitioner within the said stipulated period; and thus, acted illegally. He further submits that the respondent customs authorities have not made any final assessment within the stipulated of period 120 working days as per law and further most illegally asked the petitioner vide letter dated 10-4-2019 (Annexure-E) to deposit money for chemical examination of the imported goods from BCSIR after long days of the provisional assessment of the goods; these sort of actions of the respondents are utterly illegal, malafide, arbitrary and without sanction of law. He lastly, goes to argue that the date of provisional assessment of the goods in question on 24-10-2018 and the concerned respondents failed to make provisional assessment of the petitioner's imported goods final within of the said statutory period 120 (one twenty) working days under section 81(2) of the Act, 1969, which is a mandatory provision of law, but grossly violated by the remiss actions of the respondents, and the bank guarantee furnished by the petitioner in good faith is now at risk of sudden arbitrally encashment by the respondents. Accordingly, he submits that a direction is required to be given upon the respondent No. 1 to return/release the bank guarantee being No. 48 of 2018 dated 22-10-2018 issued by South East Bank Ltd, Corporate Branch, Dhaka in favour of the petitioner. In support of his aforesaid submissions, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the decisions of the case of Government of Bangladesh and others vs Md Salim Hossain reported in 11 BLT (AD) page 71 and Nasir Glass Industries Limited vs National Board of Revenue and others reported in 17 BLT (HCD) 243. 

11. Per contra, Mr AHM Zia Uddin, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1, Commissioner of Customs, ICD, Kamalapur, Dhaka submits that as per request of the petitioner vide letter dated 18-10-2018, the respondent customs authority made provisional assessment on 24-10-2018 and released the goods on accepting bank guarantee for the differential amount of duty and taxes and accordingly, collected sample of the goods and sent the same to BCSIR Lab on 27-11-2018 for chemical examination in order to determine the actual HS Code. But, the petitioner however, has not deposited the legally required fee for the chemical test in violation of mandatory provision of section 200 of the Act, 1969 and to that context the respondent customs authority could not assess the goods finally due to fault of the petitioner and thus, the Rule is liable to be discharged. He further submits that the goods in question have been released on provisional assessment under section 81 of the Act, 1969 and sample of the goods was sent to the BCSIR for chemical examination on 27-11-2018 and informed the BCSIR authority that the cost of test would be provided by the petitioner under the Act, 1969 and the copy of said letter forwarded to the petitioner as well as his C&F agent. But, the petitioner after being informed did not pay the required fee of sample test to the BCSIR and moreover, the respondent No. 2 vide his letter dated 10-4-2019 informed the petitioner for taking necessary steps to deposit test fee in favour of the BCSIR within 10 days but, the petitioner did not pay required fee for chemical test under the mandatory provision of section 200 of the Act, 1969 till date. As such, on failure to deposit chemical test fee by the petitioner, the provisional assessment made by the respondent customs authority on their proposed HS Code is deemed to be treated as final and the petition does not have any legal right to claim to return the bank guarantee furnished as security on provisional assessment. He further goes to argue that as request of vide letter dated 18-10-2018, the respondent No. 1 for determination of actual HS Code of the goods and send the sample to the BCSIR Lab on 27-11-2018 for chemical examination but, the petitioner did not pay the said test fee as required under the provision of section 200 of Act, 1969. Hence, such acts of the petitioner is deemed to be accepted the HS Code fixed by the customs authority and the provisional assessment made by the respondent custom authority shall be treated as final. Lastly, he goes to submit that, the petitioner filed the instant writ petition by practicing found upon the Court as well as customs authority and unclean hand, and hence, the instant Rule is liable to be discharged. 

12. Heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner, the learned Assistant Attorney-General for the respondent No. 1, have perused the writ petition, materials on record so appended thereto and relevant provision of law. 

13. The cardinal issue requires determination in the instant writ petition is that whether the petitioner is entitled to get return of the bank guarantee furnished by him at the time of releasing the goods on provisional assessment, due to failure of the respondent customs authority to make final assessment of the goods in question within the stipulated period of 120(one hundred twenty) working days, as prescribed under section 81 of the Act, 1969. 

14. In order to appreciate the respective arguments of both the parties, it is pertinent to refer to the relevant provision of law i.e. section 81 of the Act, 1969 for proper disposal of the instant Rule, which reads as under; 
"Section 81. Provisional assessment of duty.—(1) Where it is not possible immediately to assess the customs duty that may be payable on any imported goods entered for home-consumption of for warehousing or for clearance from a warehouse for home-consumption or on any goods entered for exportation, for the reason that the goods require chemical or other test (or a further enquiry( for purposes of assessment, or that all the documents or complete documents or full information pertaining to those goods have not been furnished, an officer not below that rank of (Assistant Commissioner of Customs] may order that the duty payable on such goods be assessed provisionally: 
Provided that the importer (same in the case of goods entered for warehousing) or the exporter pays such additional amount as security or furnishes such guarantee of a scheduled bank for the payment thereof as the said officer deems sufficient to meet the excess of the final assessment of duty over the provisional assessment. [(2) Where any goods are allowed to be cleared or delivered on the basis of such provisional assessment, the amount of duty actually payable on those goods shall, within a period of one hundred and twenty working days from the date of the provisional assessment, where there is a case pending at any court, tribunal or appellate authority, from the date of receipt of the final disposal order of that case, be finally assessed and on completion of such assessment the appropriate officer shall order that the amount already guaranteed be adjusted against the amount payable on the basis of final assessment, and the difference between them shall be paid forthwith to or by the importer or exporter as the case may be: 
Provided that the Board may, under exceptional circumstances recorded in writing, extend the period of final assessment specified under this sub-section." 

15. Section 81 provides that when the customs authority is of the opinion that it is not possible to assess the duty and taxes immediately that may be payable on any imported goods or any goods entered for exportation for the reason that the goods require chemical or other test for purpose of assessment or that all the documents or complete documents or full information pertaining to those goods have not been furnished, an officer not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs may order that the duty payable on such goods be assessed provisionally. The importer or exporter pays such additional amount as security or furnishes such guarantee of a schedule bank for the payment thereof as the officer seems sufficient to meet the excess of the final assessment of duty over the provisional assessment. When any goods are released on the basis of such provisionally assessment, the amount of duty actually payable on those goods shall, within a period of 120 (one hundred twenty) working days be finally assessed but where any case pending before the any Court, or authority the date for final assessment be counted from the date of receipt of the final disposal order of the case. As per proviso of this section only the Board may under exceptional circumstances recorded in writing extend the period of final assessment specified under this section. 

16. In this regard section 200 provides as under: 
"Section 200: Owner to make all arrangements and bear all expenses:—Any opening, unpacking, waiving, measuring, repacking, bulking, sorting, letting, marketing, numbering, loading, unloading, carrying or lading of goods or their containers for the purposes of, or incidental to, the examination, including any investigation, scientific or chemical test or draft survey, by an officer of Customs, removal or warehousing thereof shall be done, and any facilities or assistance required for any such examination, investigation, test or survey shall be provided, by or at the expense of the owner of the goods." 

17. Vide section 200 the owner of the goods has to make arrangement and bear all expenses of opening, unpacking, waiving, measuring, repacking, bulking, sorting, letting, marketing, . numbering, loading, unloading, carrying or lading of goods or their containers for the purposes of, or incidental to, the examination, including any investigation, scientific or chemical test or draft survey, by an officer of Customs, removal or warehousing thereof shall be done, and any facilities or assistance required for any such examination, investigation, test or survey. 

18. In the instant case, the petitioner imported "Black Steel Seamless Pipe" under HS Code Nos. 7304.29.10 and 7304.29.20 and submitted Bill of Entry No. C-28719 dated 18-10-2018 before the concerned customs authority in order to release the goods on payment of customs duty and taxes. The customs authority physically examined the goods and found that the declared HS Code was not correct and which was fallen under HS Code Nos. 7306.29.20 and 7306.29.10 respectively. In the above circumstances, the petitioner through his C&F agent on 18-10-2018 made a representation to the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chattogram requesting to release the goods on provisionally assessment by accepting bank guarantee for the differential amount of duty and taxes. Vide the said representation the petitioner also requested to draw the sample of the goods and send the same to BCSIR for chemical examination in order to determine of actual HS Code for the purpose of final assessment. Considering the said representation, the concerned customs authority made a proposal in their note sheet vide Nathi No. 5-Cus (1386) Amdani/ICD/ Group-06/2018 for approval (Annexure 2 of the affidavit-in-opposition). The relevant context of the Note Sheet runs as follows; 
“১১। নথির ডান পাশে রক্ষিত পত্র পাতা নং ২৬ সদয় দ্রষ্টব্য পত্র পাতা তে আলোচ্য পণ্য চালানের আমদানী কারক Nippon Boiler House, Dhaka । আলোচ্য পণ্য চালানটির পার্থক্য শুক্ককরাদি ব্যাংক গ্যারান্টির ভিত্তিতে সাময়িক শুল্কায়ন পূর্বক খালাশের আবেদন করেছেন । আবেদনে আমদানী কারক উল্লেখ করেন যে এইস এস কোড ৭৩০৪.২৯.২০ তে সাময়িক শুল্কায়ন করে ব্যাংক গ্যারান্টির ভিত্তিতে খালাস গ্রহণ এবং নমুনা সংগ্রহ করে রাসায়নিক পরীক্ষায় প্রেরণের জন্য আবেদন করেন। রাসায়নিক নিতে বাধ্য থাকিবে মর্মে অঙ্গীকার প্রদান করেন । এ বিষয়ে আবেদন খানা গৃহীত হলে ব্যাংক গ্যারান্টি গব্দহন পূর্বক সাময়িক শুল্কায়ন করা যেতে পারে ।”

19. Pursuant to the said proposal, the goods in question were assessed provisionally on 24-10-2018 and accordingly, released in favour of the petitioner on furnishing bank guarantee being No. 48 of 2018 amounting to Taka 15,86,504.07 for the differential amount of duty and taxes as security for the purpose of final assessment. Later, the customs authority took the sample in presence of the petitioner and the respondent No. 1, Commissioner of Customs under signature of the Assistant Commissioner of Customs sent the same to BCSIR for chemical examination on 27-11-2018 with copy to the petitioner and his C&F agent in order to take necessary steps towards payment of test fee [Annexure 2(3) to the affidavit-in-opposition J. The petitioner, however, did not make payment of chemical test fee to the concerned authority of BCSIR despite repeated requests, as was required under section 200, which is evident from the custom's Note Sheet. The relevant part of the note sheet is quoted below; 
“২০ । নোট অনুচ্ছেদ ১১ সদয় দেখা যেতে পারে । বি/ই নং ২৮৭১৯, তারিখ ১৮-১০-২০১৮ এর মাধ্যমে আমদানিকৃত পণ্যচালানটি ব্যাতক গ্যারান্টি গ্রহণ পূর্বক সাময়িকভাবে শুল্কায়ন করে খালাস প্রদান করা হয় । একই অনুচ্ছেদ মোতাবেক পণ্য চালানটির নমুনা রাসায়নিক পরীক্ষণে প্রেরণের প্রস্তাব অনুমোদিত হয়। এমতাবস্থায় পণ্যচালানটির নমুনা রাসায়নিক পরীক্ষণের জন্য প্রেরণের লক্ষ্যে প্রেরিত পত্রের খসড়া সহ নথিটি উপস্থাপন করা হলো।
স্বাঃ
তারিখঃ ২৭-১১-২০১৮ ইং
২১। নোট অনুচ্ছেদ ২০ এর নির্দেশনা মোতাবেক নমুনা প্রেরণ পূর্বক রিসিভ কপি পৃঃপত্র তে রক্ষিত রয়েছে। সদয় অবগতির লক্ষ্যে উপস্থাপিত।
স্বাঃ
তারিখঃ ২৭-১১-২০১৮ ইং
২২। নোটানুচ্ছেদ নং ২১ এর আলোকে গত ২৭-১১-২০১৮ তারিখ গবেষণা সমন্বয়কারী, বিসিএসআইআর, বাংলাদেশ বিজ্ঞান ও শিল্প গবেষণালয়, ড. কুদরত-ই-খুদা রোড, ধানমন্ডি, ঢাকা বরাবর সংশ্লিষ্ট পণ্যের নমুনা রাসায়নিক পরীক্ষার জন্য প্রেরণ করা হয়। উক্ত রাসায়নিক পরীক্ষার ফি সরকারী নিয়ম অনুযায়ী সংশ্লিষ্ট আমাদানিকারকের পরিশোধের বিধান থাকলেও, আমদানিকারককে এ বিষয়ে পত্র মারফত অবহিত করা স্বত্ত্বেও তিনি রাসায়নিক পরীক্ষার ফি প্রদান করেননি ।
২৩ । আলোচ্য রাসায়নিক পরীক্ষার ফি প্রদানের জন্য আমদানিকারককে পুনরায় পত্র মারফত জানানো যেতে পারে। প্রেরিতব্য পত্রের খসড়া/খচ্ছ কপি সদয় অনুমোদন ও স্বাক্ষরের জন্য নথি সবিনয়ে উপস্থাপিত।
স্বাঃ
তারিখঃ ১০-৪-২০১৯
 
20. Consequently, the customs authority failed to collect test report from BCSIR and could not make final assessment of the goods in question within the time, as required under section 81(2) of the Act. In this connection it is pertinent to note that the respondent customs authority had initiated process for chemical test of the goods within the specified time for the purpose of final assessment. Under the stated circumstances, we have no manner of doubt to find that the petitioner is fully responsible for the said delay which has occurred due to his willful negligence and malafide conduct. In the given context failure on the part of the respondent customs authorities to make final assessment of the goods in question within time cannot be termed as unlawful. 

21. Another assertion of the petitioner is that the respondent customs authority asked the petitioner to pay the chemical test fee vide letter dated 10-4-2019 after expiry of 120(one hundred twenty) working days. Said assertion is a misconceived one for, the respondent No. 1, Commissioner of Customs under the signature of the Deputy Commissioner of Customs vide office letter dated 10-4-2019 further requested the petitioner to take necessary steps to collect test report from BCSIR for the purpose of making final assessment and that said letter was issued pursuant to the earlier office letter dated 27-11-2018, requesting the petitioner to arrange payment of test fees. The petitioner without complying the said request filed the instant writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution with unclean hand. 

22. Considering the context given herein above we are of the view that, due to negligence and malafide conduct on the part of any importer/exporter, if the customs authority fails to make provisional assessment final, the value/HS Code fixed by the customs authority of any imported/exported goods for the purpose of assessment shall be deemed to have been accepted by such importer/exporter and the provisional assessment so made by the customs authority on the basis of their fixation value/HS Code shall be deemed to be treated as final. Consequently, the concerned customs authority is at liberty to encash the bank guarantee(s) after expiry of the statutory period of 120 (one hundred twenty) working days as prescribed under section 81(2) of the Act. 

23. In the decisions so referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner as well as in earlier judgments along with the judgment passed by this Court in writ petition No. 4006 of 2019 (we are both parties to that judgment) it has been observed inter alia; 
"In view of the statutory provision of law and the ratio settled by our Apex Court, we are of the view that on the failure of the customs authority to complete provisional assessment as final within the statutory period of 120(one hundred twenty) working days as prescribed under section 81(2) of the Act, 1969 or failure to extend the said period for final assessment from the Board, the provisional assessment made by the customs authority on the basis of declared value/ H.S Code shall be deemed as final. Consequent thereof the concerned importer/exporter is entitled to get return the bank guarantee(s) furnished by him as security on provisional assessment."

24. The aforesaid ratio has been settled by this Court relying on the fact of the cases that when on failure to complete provisional assessment as final within the prescribed period under section 81(2) of the Act, 1969 due to conduct or negligence on part of the customs authorities, not on part of the any importer/ exporter. So, the facts and circumstances of the cases referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner being distinguishable are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. 

25. However, in the present case, "due to willful negligence on part of the petitioner to pay chemical examination expenses fee to the BCSIR as required under section 200 of the Act, the respondent customs authority did not collect the test report for the purpose of final assessment of the goods in question. Such acts of the petitioner are not tenable in the eye of law. Consequently, the petitioner is barred from seeking any relief under Article 102 of the Constitution on the plea that the final assessment has/had not been done by the customs authority within 120(one hundred twenty) working days as prescribed under section 81(2) of the Act, 1969". 

26. Resulting, the petitioner looses his right to seek to return of the bank guarantee as furnished by him an provisional assessment. 

27. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, findings and observations so given herein above, we find no substance in the instant Rule. 

28. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged. 

29. The order of status quo granted earlier by this Court is hereby recalled and vacated. 

30. The concerned respondent is at liberty to encash the bank guarantee furnished by the petitioner on provisional assessment. 

31. There will be no order as to costs. 

Communicate the copy of this judgment and order to the concerned respondents forthwith. 

End.

full_judgment:
Naima Haider, J: In this Application under Article 102 of the Constitution, a Rule Nisi was issued in the following terms: 
Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the amended Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (Officers and Staffs) Recruitment Rules, 1992 published in the gazette notification dated 9-5-2016 (Annexure-E) shall not be declared ultra vires to the Constitution so far as it relates to the petitioners and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The instant writ petition is elaborately drafted with certain information which are not strictly relevant to the disposal of the instant Rule. Therefore, we are not inclined to set out elaborate facts. 

3. The petitioners are law abiding citizens of Bangladesh. They are second class officers working for Bangladesh Road Transport Authority as Motor Vehicle Inspectors, carrying out responsibilities set out under the Motor Vehicle Ordinance 1983 ("1983 Ordinance") and the Motor Vehicles Rules 1984. Bangladesh Road Transport Authority was established under section 2(A)(1) of the 1983 Ordinance through SRO No. 303-Law/87. The petitioners were appointed to carry out the functions relating to, among others, registration of motor vehicles, providing driving licence etc. The petitioners who were directly appointed had the requisite qualifications as set out in the schedule of-  
বাংলাদেশ রোড ট্রান্সপোর্ট অথরিটি (কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা-১৯৯২ being “সরাসরি নিয়োগের ক্ষেত্রে বাংলাদেশ কারিগরী শিক্ষা বোর্ড কর্তৃক অনুমোদিত অটোমোবাইলস/পাওয়ার টেকনোসজিতে ৩ (তিন) বুসর মেয়াদী ডিপ্লোমা অথবা উহার সমমানের ডিপ্লোম পরীক্ষায় উত্তীর্ণ এবং তৎসহ অন্যুন ৩ (তিন) বৎসরের চাকুরী।

4. The main grievance of the petitioners are as follows: In the বাংলাদেশ রোড ট্রান্সপোর্ট অথরিটি (কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা-১৯৯২ the petitioners were placed in serial No.11. Revenue Officer was in serial No. 10 while প্রধান সহকারী was in serial No. 12. There was no post of Assistant Revenue Officers. By the impugned amendment, a new post was created and the petitioners were allocated serial No.31 while the Assistant Revenue Officers were allocated serial No. 30 but the post of প্রধান সহকারী remained immediately below the petitioners, as was before. According to the petitioners, the respondents by placing Assistant Revenue Officers to a post higher than that of the petitioners committed illegality which should be remedied by this Division. It was further submitted that by the impugned amendment, the eligibility criteria for promotion was also changed. According to the learned Counsel, such amendments are not binding on the petitioners as they have been appointed and/or been rendering services under the original বাংলাদেশ রোড ট্রান্সপোর্ট অথরিটি (কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা-১৯৯২. The petitioners are also aggrieved by the order issued by the respondents allowing User ID, password and approval panel to the Assistant Revenue Officers in the computerized system of BRTA on experimental basis. According to the petitioners, this is contradictory to the provisions of the Motor Vehicle Ordinance 1983 and the Rules framed thereunder. The petitioners also contend that given the nature of the job, it is necessary to have the eligibility criteria set out the schedule of reproduced above; however by the impugned amendment the eligibility criteria was modified and the requirement of practical work experience had been omitted. 

5. Assistant Revenue Officers filed an Application for Addition of Party. This 
Division, allowed the said application and added the Assistant Revenue Officers as respondent Nos.8-28 in the instant writ petition since they were necessary and proper parties to the proceedings. 

6. The Rule was opposed. Two separate Affidavits-in-Opposition were filed by respondent No.4 and respondent Nos. 8-28. The learned Counsel appearing for the respondent No.4-Bangladesh Road Transport Authority, takes us through the Affidavit-in-Opposition and submits that the petitioners and Assistant Revenue Officers are holding equivalent posts and holding the same status having similar pay scales. The learned Counsel submits that the amendment to the বাংলাদেশ রোড ট্রান্সপোর্ট অথরিটি (কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা-১৯৯২ does not, in any way curtail the rights and privileges of the petitioners and therefore, the instant writ petition is misconceived. The relevant part of the Affidavit-in-Opposition is reproduced for ease of reference "...It is stated by this respondent that the posts of Motor Vehicle Inspectors and the Assistant Revenue Officers are equivalent posts; holding same status and their pay scale are similar. It is further stated that an amended gazette notification of Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (Officers and Staffs) Recruitment Rules 1992 was published on 9-5-2016 wherein the post of the petitioners are placing in serial No.31 immediately below the post of Assistant Revenue Officers (Serial No. 30) as the petitioners and the Assistant Revenue Officers are holding equivalent posts of second class officers, same status and having same pay scale and, as such, the post of the petitioners could not be place d in the serial No. 30 with the posts of Assistant Revenue Officers and hence, the same was placed in serial No. 31, the rights and privileges of the petitioners granted by the original recruitment Rules neither curtailed nor prevented...". The learned Counsel further submits that the respondents adopted a resolution and decided to create user ID and password for Assistant Revenue Officers of BRTA so that they can report to the authority properly. The learned Counsel further submits that the amendment, impugned by the petitioners, have been made following due process of law and the amendment was to ensure that the authority can operate properly and therefore, there is nothing wrong with the amendments, as alleged or at all. On these counts, the learned Counsel submits that the instant Rule should be discharged. 

7. The learned Counsel appearing for respondent Nos. 8-28 takes us through the Affidavit-in-Opposition and makes elaborate submissions, especially by reference to paragraph No.10, on the allocation of business of the Assistant Revenue Officers and the Motor Vehicle Inspectors. According to the learned Counsel, the functions of the posts are different and therefore, no illegality was committed by the respondent-BRTA in issuing the impugned amended Rules. The learned Counsel further submits that if a new post is created, there is no requirement that the new post must be placed in accordance with the Government GO. He further refers to the organogram of the respondent-BRTA to show that the reporting lines of Assistant Revenue Officers and Motor Vehicle Inspectors are different; consequentially, it was necessary to place them in different serials. He further submits that it was necessary that the added respondents be provided with the pass words and IDs so that they can perform their functions properly. The learned Counsel also submits that the petitioners have failed to show how the impugned amendment is illegal and therefore, on this, among other counts, he submits that the instant Rule should be discharged. It is to be mentioned that the learned Counsel for the added respondents did not take any stance different from that taken by the respondent No.4-BRTA. 

8. We have heard the learned Counsels for the petitioners and the respondents. We have also perused the writ petition and the Affidavits in Opposition 'and the documents annexed therein. 

9. At the outset, we would like to point out that this Division has certain limitations in exercising its powers under Article 102 of the Constitution. This Division, in exercise of powers under the Constitution, should not interfere with the internal affairs of an executive authority. By this, we mean that this Division should be reluctant to interfere with allocation of functions within an executive authority, unless, the allocation of functions is illegal or manifestly arbitrary or is such that the same could be regarded as "absurd". In the instant case, the post of Assistant Revenue Officers was created by the impugned amendment and the officers were assigned certain duties. We are not inclined to interfere on whether the allocation was proper as the learned Counsel for the petitioner could not show any of the exceptional circumstances which would justify our interference. 

10. We have taken a note that the respondent No.4, through affidavit confirmed that the posts of Assistant Revenue Officers and the Motor Vehicle Inspectors stand on the same footing, for all material purposes. Since both cannot be placed under the same serial, both the posts had to be under two separate serials. We are not fully convinced with this argument. By the impugned Gazette Notification dated 9-5-2016, certain amendments were made to বাংলাদেশ রোড ট্রান্সপোর্ট অথরিটি (কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা-১৯৯২. The Schedule to the বাংলাদেশ রোড ট্রান্সপোর্ট অথরিটি (কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা-১৯৯২ was substituted. We note a pattern of hierarchy in the Schedule. For instance, Directors appears above the Deputy Directors and the Deputy Directors appear above the Assistant Directors etc. By that analogy, Assistant Revenue Officers have higher standing than that of the petitioners. 

11. To understand whether the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the respondent No.4 has any merit, we had perused the Warrant of Precedence (Revised up to December 2003) as an aid to our interpretation. The Warrant of Precedence sets out the hierarchy. For instance the Hon'ble President is ranked No.1 and the Hon'ble Prime Minister is ranked No.2. However, when different persons have same status, their designations are set out in the same serial. Under the Warrant of Precedence, Cabinet Minister, Deputy Speaker of the Parliament, Leader of the Opposition have the same rank. All of them rank under the same serial being serial No. 5. Likewise, Election Commissioners and the Judges of the Supreme Court (High Court Division) rank equally and are placed under serial No.9. Thus, when within a Authority, there are different posts ranking similar in all respects, these posts should be placed in the organogram under the same serial. 

12. Even if we take the argument of the learned Counsel for the respondents that the petitioners and Assistant Revenue Officers rank the same in all aspects, in our view, they should have been in the same serial. It was wrong to create a separate serial, one for the petitioners and one for Assistant Revenue Officers who, according to the respondent No.4 are ranked equally. The different raking creates confusion and most certainly, gives a wrong impression about the hierarchy. That being the position, relying on the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for respondent No.4, we are inclined to hold that a direction should be passed by this Division to place both the petitioners and the Assistant Revenue Officers under the same serial. Consequentially, the respondents should be directed to take steps in this regard. 

13. Now, let us examine the nature of the two posts. The post of Assistant Revenue Officers have been recently created while the post of the petitioners were in the original schedule to বাংলাদেশ রোড ট্রান্সপোর্ট অথরিটি (কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা-১৯৯২.

14. In the বাংলাদেশ রোড ট্রান্সপোর্ট অথরিটি (কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা-১৯৯২ the petitioners were placed in serial No.11. Revenue Officer was in serial No. 10 while প্রধান সহকারী was in serial No. 12. There was no post of Assistant Revenue Officers. By the impugned amendment, a new post was created and the petitioners were allocated serial No.31 while the Assistant Revenue Officers were allocated serial No.30 but the post of প্রধান সহকারী remained immediately below the petitioners, as was before. 

15. Under the original Schedule, প্রধান সহকারী writ was promoted to Revenue Officer. However, under the impugned amended Schedule, প্রধান সহকারী is promoted to Assistant Revenue Officer. If under the old schedule, which regulated the terms and conditions of service of the petitioners, Revenue Officers were immediately above the post of the petitioners, in our view, the post of Assistant Revenue Officers cannot be regarded as superior to that of Motor Vehicle Inspectors. 

16. Therefore, we are of the view that the petitioners should be placed before the Assistant Revenue Officers while placing both the petitioners and the Assistant Revenue Officers under the same serial in light of our observation above. 

17. Before we part with the judgment, we would also like to point out that the terms of service of the petitioners were regulated under the provisions of the previous বাংলাদেশ রোড ট্রান্সপোর্ট অথরিটি (কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা-১৯৯২. The impugned amendments made certain changes to the eligibility criteria for promotion. Since the petitioners were rendering the services under the provisions of the original বাংলাদেশ রোড ট্রান্সপোর্ট অথরিটি (কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা-১৯৯২, the impugned amendments would not be applicable in respect of the petitioners. 

18. We would also like to point out that the nature of petitioners' job requires specialized skills and it seems desirable and proper that a candidate for the post of Motor Vehicle Inspectors have both requisite educational practical work experience. Therefore, the impugned amendment which no longer requires practical work experience for direct appointment to the post of Motor Vehicle Inspectors is erroneous. We are of the view that the respondents should take steps to ensure that work experience of 3(three) years (তৎসহ অন্যুন ৩ (তিন) বৎসরের চাকুরী) is also made mandatory for direct appointment as was originally required. 

19. In light of the aforesaid discussions, we are inclined to dispose of the instant writ petition with the following direction and observation: 
(a) The respondents are directed to place the petitioners and the Assistant Revenue Officers under the same serial in the amended Schedule and in doing so, the respondents are further directed to ensure that Motor Vehicle Inspectors are placed above the Assistant Revenue Officers; 
(b) The respondents should take steps to ensure that work experience of 3 (three) years (তৎসহ অন্যুন ৩ (তিন) বৎসরের চাকুরী) is also made mandatory for direct appointment of Motor Vehicle Inspectors as was originally required; 
(c) The provisions of the amended বাংলাদেশ রোড ট্রান্সপোর্ট অথরিটি (কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা-১৯৯২ particularly the part of the Schedule which deals with the eligibility criteria for promotion shall not be applicable in case of the petitioners since the petitioners had been appointed and/or rendering 
service under the provisions of the original বাংলাদেশ রোড ট্রান্সপোর্ট অথরিটি (কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা-১৯৯২ .

Communicate the Judgment and Order at once for immediate compliance. 

End.

lawyer:
Bikash Paul, Advocate—For the Plaintiff-Petitioner. 
M. Mushfiqur Rahman with Nahid Sultana Jenny, Advocates—For the added Responded-Opposite Party Nos. 4 & 5.
parties:
Saleha Khatoon ------ Plaintiff-petitioner
vs
Mistu Begum and others Defendant ----- opposite parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 23-4-2019 passed by the learned District Judge, Narsingdi in Title Appeal No. 44 of 2016 allowing the application under Order I, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for addition party should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Material facts relevant for disposal of this Rule, briefly, are that the petitioner as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 73 of 2006 in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge for specific performance of contract against the defendant opposite parties. Ultimately, the suit was decreed on contest by the judgment and decree dated 25-1-2016. Against which the defendant, Mst. Misti Begum filed Title Appeal No. 44 of 2016 before the learned District Judge, Narsingdi and thereafter, while the appeal was in progress the added opposite party Nos. 4 & 5 namely, Sheikh Delwar Hossain and Md Asaduzzaman Tipu filed an application under Order I, rule 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for addition of party stating, inter-alia, that they purchased the suit land within the full knowledge of the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 73 of 2006 and others by 2 registered deeds dated 6-9-2016 and on the same date the vendor handed over possession of the said land to them and since then they have been paying rent and taxes to the Government. The added opposite party Nos. 4-5 in the month of November, 2017 for the first time came to know that a suit being Civil Suit No. 73 of 2006 for specific performance of contract in respect of their land has been decreed in which they are in possession and against the said decree the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 44 of 2016, which is now pending before the learned District Judge, Narsingdi and in the attending facts and circumstances they have direct interest over the suit land and that they may be added as parties in the appeal for adequate disposal of the appeal. 

3. The learned District Judge, Narsingdi after hearing both the sides by his order dated 23-4-2019 allowed the application for addition of party on the finding that in the facts and circumstances of the case if the applicants are not made parties there is possibility of multiplicity of suits. 

4. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid order dated 23-4-2019 passed by the learned District Judge, Narsingdi the plaintiff petitioners have come before this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

5. Mr Biksh Kumar Paul, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners in the course of his argument takes me through the revisional application and other materials on record and then submits that admittedly, the plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance of contract and the learned Assistant Judge on due consideration of the entire materials on record factually found the plaintiff has succeeded to prove his case and accordingly decreed the suit and thereafter, the defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 44 of 2016 and while the appeal was in progress the stranger purchasers all on a sudden filed an application under Order I, rule 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for addition of parties stating that they purchased total 19.5 decimals of land out of which 18.5 decimals of land is related with the suit land and it is on record that the stranger purchasers are in no way connected or parties to the agreement of bainanama in question and the Court of appeal below without applying its judicial mind into the facts and circumstance of the case and law bearing on the subject most illegally allowed the applicants to be added as the respondent Nos. 4-5. Finally, the learned Advocate relying on the decisions reported in 43 DLR (AD) 107, 19 BLD (HC) 485, 24 BLD (AD) 47, 14 BLT (AD) 16, 58 DLR 62, 13 BLT (AD) 206, 9 BLC (AD) 114, 8 BLT (AD) 301 submits that since the added opposite parties purchased a part of the suit land during pendency of the suit and it is on record that they are not parties to the agreement in question and they cannot be made party in the appeal or suit and in this case there is no special circumstances in which the opposite parties can be added as parties to fortify their case although the Court of appeal below without applying its judicial mind into the facts and circumstances of the case mechanically allowed the prayer for addition of party, which resulted in the failure of justice. 

6. Mr M. Mushfiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the added opposite party Nos. 4-5, on the other hand, supports the impugned order, which was according to him just, correct and proper. The learned Advocate at the very outset points out that in this case though the petitioner challenged the order of the learned District Judge dated 23-4-2019 allowing the application for addition of party under Order I, rule 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure but the plaintiff petitioner deliberately with unclean hands did not implead the added opposite parties in this revisional application and the added opposite parties on knowing about the instant revisional application arising out from the order dated 23-4-2019 allowing the prayer for addition of party filed an application again before this Court for addition of party and this Court by order dated 11-2-2020 allowed the prayer for addition of party and in that facts and circumstances of the case it can safely be said that the petitioner did not approach before this Court with clean hands. The learned Advocate next relying on a number of decisions namely the decisions reported in 7 BLT (AD) 103, 3 BLD (AD) 268, 53 DLR (AD) 45, 15 BLD (AD) 95, 15 MLR (HCD) 409, .54 DLR 223, 35 DLR 110 submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract a stranger to the contract in question can be added as a party for proper adjudication of the suit under special circumstances. The learned Advocate next points out that the Court of appeal below on due consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case rightly held that-
"The case of the petitioners clearly comes within the exception of the general principle of addition of party in a suit for specific performance of contract and they are proper parties to be added as defendants in the suit for proper adjudication of the real dispute as to whether the disputed bainapatra in question is a forged, fake or genuine one. Furthermore, it can be said that although it is the general rule that the parties to the contract against whom the performance is sought are the necessary parties to the suit, but there may have exceptional circumstances where the question of forgery raises as to the deed of contract for sale and where the third parties claim that they are in possession of the suit land. If find such kind of exceptions in the instant case." 

7. And, on this findings allowed the prayer for addition of party. The learned Advocate further submits that since in this case special circumstances are there that the purchasers of the suit land after purchasing the land in question mutated their name in the suit land and developed the suit property and have been residing therein peacefully and in such facts and circumstances the defendant Nos. 1-3 after transfer of the suit land have lost their interest and thereupon, the present added opposite parties to protect their interest and for proper adjudication of the matter are the necessary parties in the suit in the interest of justice. Finally, the learned Advocate submits that there is nothing on record to show that the added opposite parties have/had any knowledge as to pending suit No. 73 of 2006 for specific performance of contract before purchasing the suit property and the plaintiff-petitioner transferred a part of the suit property without disclosing as to pending suit and, as such, the decisions reported in 9 BLC (AD) 115 is not applicable in the present case. 

8. 1 have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for both the sides and perused the Civil Revision application and the impugned order and other materials on record as filed thereto. 

9. The only question for consideration is, whether the Court of appeal below correctly held that case of the applicants clearly comes within the exception of the general principle of addition of party in a suit for specific performance of contract and they are proper parties to be added as defendants in the suit for proper adjudication of the real dispute as to whether the disputed bainapatra in question is a forged, fake or genuine one. 

10. In deciding this point, I have carefully gone through the cited decisions to the best of my ability and find a clear view law as it stands today that in a special circumstance a third party to a contract can be added as party to a suit for specific performance of contract. In this case, I have already noticed that the added opposite parties during pendency of the Civil Suit No. 73 of 2006 purchased a part of the suit land beyond their knowledge as to the fact that a civil suit is pending in respect of the suit property and after purchasing the suit property they mutated their name and started living thereon by constructing a road. The proposition of law is by now well settled that under the special circumstance for the purpose of a complete and effective adjudication of the dispute and to avoid multiplicity of suit even a stranger may be added as party to a suit for specific performance of contract. In this case the learned District Judge on due consideration of the facts and attending circumstances came to the conclusion that—
"the case of the applicants clearly comes within the exception of the general principle of addition of party in a suit for specific performance of contract and they are proper parties to be added as defendant in the suit for proper adjudication of the real dispute as to whether the disputed bainapatra in question is a forged, fake or genuine one Under such circumstance if the petitioners are not made party in the original suit there is possibility of multiplicity of proceedings." 

11. This finding of the Court of appeal below certainly indicates that the Court of appeal below considered the material fact that whether there are special circumstance exist or not and factually found that the clear existence of exception of the general principle for addition of party in a suit for specific performance of contract. 

12. In the fact and circumstances and the position of the case as I have discussed above, I do not find any reason to differ with the view taken by the learned District Judge, Narsingdi. 

13. The learned District Judge, Narsingdi having decided the matter on due consideration of the materials on record and in accordance with law, the same calls for no interference. 

14. I have carefully gone through the decisions cited by Mr Bikash Paul, the learned Advocate for the Plaintiff-petitioner and find that the principles as enunciated in those decisions have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case inasmuch as facts of those cases are quite distinguishable from the facts of the present case. Every case shall be considered in the facts and circumstances of that case only. 

15. In view of my discussions made in the foregoing paragraphs it is by now clear that the instant Rule must fail. 

16. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated. The appellate Court concerned, will, however, expedite the hearing of the appeal. 

Let a copy of this judgment be communicated to the Court concerned at once. 

End.

lawyer: For Appellant/Petitioner/Plaintiff: Md. Asaduzzaman, Advocate instructed by Syed Mahbubur Rahman, Advocate-on-Record
parties:
Appellants: Zahid Hossain and Ors.
Vs.
Respondent: Syed Fazlul Kader and Ors.
case_source: From the Judgment And Order dated 12.02.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3795 of 2003
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique, J.
1. This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 12.02.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3795 of 2003 affirming the judgment and decree dated 02.06.2003 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Fifth Court, Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 187 of 1997 affirming those dated 25.03.1997 passed by the then learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 127 of 1993.

2. The plaintiff-respondents instituted Title Suit No. 37 of 1979 in the Third Court of the then Subordinate Judge, Chittagong, impleading the defendants praying for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of the suit land. The plaintiff's case, in short, was that the suit land originally belonged to one Ramzan Ali, who died leaving two sons, Abdul Wahab alias Thanda Miah and Gura Miah as his legal heirs. Gura Miah died leaving one son, Md. Yusuf. Thanda Miah died leaving one son Fazlul Haque as their respective heirs. Md. Yusuf sold his share of the suit land to Fazlul Haque by a deed of sale dated 19.06.1978 and, thus, Fazlul Haue became the sole owner of the entire suit property. The R.S. and P.S. Khatians in respect of the suit land were correctly prepared and published in the name of Fazlul Haque. He executed and registered deeds of sale dated 20.07.1978, 24.07.1978, 27.07.1978 and 28.07.1978 in respect of the suit land to the plaintiffs. They mutated their names and accordingly Mutation Khatian No. 285/1 was opened. Prior to such purchase, the plaintiffs had published a notice in a daily newspaper. On 25.12.1978, the defendants forcibly dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land and made barbed wire fencing surrounding the same. The plaintiffs requested the defendants to restore possession of the suit land but of no avail. Thus, they were compelled to file the suit.

3. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending that the suit land originally belonged to Ramzan Ali who died leaving behind three sons, Kala Miah, Abdul Wahab alias Thanda Miah and Gura Miah. Abdul Wahab died leaving behind his only son Fazlul Haque. Gura Miah died leaving his only son Md. Yusuf. Kala Miah, Fazlul Haque and Md. Yusuf sold the suit land to the father of defendant Nos. 1 to 4, late Zakir Hossain, the then Governor of erstwhile East Pakistan by a registered deed of sale dated 24.06.1960. Zakir Hossain went to possession of the same. Zakir Hossain died leaving the defendants Nos. 1 to 4 who have been possessing the suit land. At the time of the alleged sale to the plaintiffs their vendor had no subsisting right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. The suit should be dismissed.

4. The trial Court decreed the suit. The defendant No. 1 preferred appeal which was dismissed. Then, the defendant No. 1 filed civil revisional application in the High Court Division and obtained Rule. The High Court Division, by the impugned judgment and order, discharged the Rule.

5. Thus, the defendants have preferred this appeal upon getting leave.

6. Mr. Md. Asaduzzaman, learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the plaintiffs filed the instant suit for declaration of their title and recovery of khas possession so it was the duty of the plaintiffs to prove that they acquired valid title on the basis of their title deeds and was in possession till the date of dispossession. But the plaintiffs have hopelessly failed to prove their title as well as possession and the story of dispossession, the learned Courts below committed error of law in decreeing the suit. He submits that the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 1-4 purchased the suit land on the basis of a sale deed dated 20.06.1960 from the admitted owners and title of the admitted owners was divested to predecessor-in-interest of the defendants on 20.06.1960 so the plaintiffs' vendor have had no subsisting interest to transfer the suit land to the plaintiffs, the learned Courts below erred in law in decreeing the suit.

7. Mr. A.M. Aminuddin, learned Senior Counsel with Mr. Qumrul Haque Siddique, learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 2, submits that the deed executed on 20.06.1960 and registered on 24.06.1960 of the defendants had not been acted upon and the same was mere paper transaction since the defendants' predecessor, after purchasing the suit land, did not mutate his name in the Khatian and in subsequent survey operation the same was recorded in the name of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs, and the defendants were not in possession till the date of dispossession of the plaintiffs. Mr. Siddique submits that as per provision of 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the record of right has got a presumptive value like presumption under Section 103(B) of Bengal Tenancy Act and that since the subsequent survey operation the suit land was recorded in the name of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs and they paid rent, it is to be presumed that the plaintiffs were in possession till the date of dispossession, the learned Courts below rightly decreed the suit. He submits that at the time of purchasing the suit land, the plaintiffs published an advertisement in the daily newspaper stating about the story of proposed sale of the suit land but the defendants did not raise any objection which indicated that the defendants had no interest in the suit land.

8. Admittedly, the suit land originally belonged to Ramzan Ali. It is the case of the plaintiffs that Ramzan Ali died leaving two sons. The contesting defendants stated that Ramzan Ali had three sons who transferred the suit land to Zakir Hossain by a deed dated 24.06.1960. It is the simple case of the plaintiffs that the said deed was not acted upon. It is the case of the plaintiffs that they purchased the suit land on 20.07.1978 and 28.07.1978 and defendants dispossessed them from the suit land on 25.12.1978. That is, admittedly, the defendants have been possessing the suit land. It is not disputed that the defendants' sale deed dated 24.04.1960 is a valid document and the same was duly stamped, executed and registered. The Court admitted the said deed in evidence without objection. Since the defendants have been possessing the suit land acting upon the said kabala deed, it is difficult to say that the defendants predecessor after purchase did not take any step pursuant to the said deed. Since the defendants have been possessing the suit land acquiring title in the same on the basis of the deed dated 24.06.1960, the submission of the plaintiffs that the kabala deed dated 24.06.1960 had not been acted upon is not acceptable. Using the deed, they performed something, so it cannot be said that the deed has yet to be acted upon.

9. The submission of Mr. Siddique is that since is revisional survey operation the suit land was recorded in the name of the plaintiffs' predecessor and they have been paying rent to the Government which has got a presumptive value as to possession, so it is to be presumed that the plaintiffs' predecessors were in possession at the time of transfer by them to the plaintiffs on 20.07.1978. The presumption as regards the entries in the R.S. Khatian so attached under Section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is rebuttable by leading evidence from the side of the person questioning correctness of entry made therein. [Govt. Vs. AKM Abdul Hye and others, 56 DLR(AD)53]

10. In order to succeed, the plaintiffs must prove that they are the persons entitled to get possession and that they had possession before the defendants took over possession. The plaintiffs did not examine any witness who executed their kabala deeds of 1978 to establish that they were in possession at the time of transfer of the suit land. The plaintiffs claimed that their predecessors were in possession through a চাষা, namely, Abul Hossain. He had not been examined to substantiate such claim. P.W. 1 in his cross-examination said “২৫-১২-১৯৭৮ইং তারিখে বিবাদীগণ কাঁটাতার দিয়া আমারে নালিশী জমি ঘিরে ফেলেছে। আমি সেই সময় উপস্থিত ছিলাম না। নালিশী জমি বিবাদীগণের বাড়ীর ভিটার সংলগ্ন এবং এই সুযোগে তারা নালিশী জমি কাটা তার দিয়ে ঘিরে ফেলেছে।”. That is, at the time of alleged dispossession, P.W. 1, who is plaintiff No. 1 and son of plaintiff No. 2, was not present. He also admitted that the suit land is the contiguous land of the "bhiti" of the defendants. It is unlikely that the defendants' predecessor, who was the Governor of the East Pakistan, after purchasing the suit land on 24.06.1960 would not take over possession of the suit land which is contiguous to his "bhiti". P.W. 1 in his cross-examination further said, “এই জমি আমরা খরিদের পূর্বে তাতে ফজলুল হকের দখল ছিল।”. To substantiate such claim they did not examine Fazlul Haque to prove the possession of Fazlul Hauqe. In his cross-examination, he further said, “এই সম্পত্তি সংক্রান্ত বিজ্ঞ ২য় সহকারী জজ আদালতে নিষেধাজ্ঞার জন্য অন্য একটি মোকদ্দমা করিয়াছিলাম ও তা খারিজ হয়েছে।” That is before filing the instant suit, they filed suit for permanent injunction and lost. In his cross-examination he further said, “জাহিদ হোসেন আমাকে নালিশী জমি থেকে বেদখল করিয়াছে, ২৫-১২-১৯৭৮ইং তারিখের বিবাদী জাহিদ হোসেন আমাকে বেদখল করেছে। সেই সময় আমি উপস্থিত ছিলাম না, সেই সময় আমার চাষা আবুল হোসেন উপস্থিত ছিল।” We have already found that Abul Hossain had not been examined. P.W. 2, Syed Jamal Ahmed in his evidence said, “বাদীগণ দখলে থাকা কালে ১৯৭৮ইং সনের ডিসেম্বর মাসের কাঁটা তারের বেড়া দিয়া তাদের বাউন্ডারীর ভিতরে নিয়া যায়।” That is, the suit land is situated within the boundary of the defendants, surrounded by barbed wire fencing. In his cross-examination he said, “নালিশী জায়গায় আমি সর্ব প্রথম ১৯৭৮ইং সনে খরিদের পর গেছি।” He further said, “কাঁটা তারের বেড়া দেওয়ার সময় আমি উপস্থিত ছিলাম না।” From the evidence of the witnesses of the plaintiffs, it appears that they went to the disputed land for the first time in 1978. They had no knowledge about the possession of the suit land before 1978. The learned Courts below while making conclusion as to title, possession and then dispossession failed to consider evidence quoted above. The learned Courts below forgot the cardinal principle that in a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession on the strength of title, the plaintiffs can succeed on establishing their title to the scheduled property and they cannot succeed on the weakness of the case put forward by the defendants. Only weakness of the defendants is that they failed to mutate their names in the khatian and paid rent which did not extinguish their title.

11. From the evidence discussion and quoted above, it appears that the plaintiffs have hopelessly failed to prove their possession till the date of alleged dispossession in the suit land and that their predecessors were in possession of the suit land before their alleged purchases. The defendants have been possessing the suit land on the basis of their deed dated 24.06.1960.

12. The plaintiffs traced their title in the suit land through their vendor who had no saleable interest after execution and registration of the deed by their predecessor on 24.06.1960. We are of the view that the defendants' deed was acted upon and that since the plaintiffs hopelessly failed to prove their possession and dispossession, they are not entitled to get relief for declaration of their title as well as recovery of possession in the suit land, the learned Courts below committed an error of law in decreeing the suit.

13. Accordingly, we find merit in the instant appeal.

14. Thus, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Courts below are hereby set aside.

End.
